findings.title: Execution authority is inherited from untrusted producers: the audited repo and the model's own output both decide what code runs, in-process and via shell
findings.summary: Raised by one perspective (adversary) and admitted on evidence, not consensus: it is the highest-impact finding in the review. The unstated, false assumption is that the things which SUPPLY the tool — the repository under audit, and the LLM output the tool consumes — are trusted to determine what executes. The tool rigorously validates the SHAPE of producer output (schemas, grounding, reviewed_clean) and never asks whether a producer has the authority to cause execution. Six verified instances, one defect class. (a) In-process import() of repo JavaScript: resolveAnalyzerDep prefers the AUDITED repo's node_modules before the shared cache (src/shared/tooling/analyzerDeps.ts:121-126), that path becomes dependencyPath (graphEnrichmentExecutor.ts:126), and typescript.ts:40-51 reads the repo's typescript/package.json, takes manifest.main, and awaits import(pathToFileURL(...)) — unsandboxed, in the auditor's process, with the entry field attacker-controlled and fed to resolve/join so it need not stay inside the package; treeSitter.ts:70-85 does the same. The wrapping try/catch (graphEnrichmentExecutor.ts:134-140) turns any throw into a cosmetic analyzer note, so a payload that runs and then throws reads as benign degradation. This is the DEFAULT path — settingFor yields auto when unset (registry.ts:66-71) and the conversation-first rule means the user sets no flags. (b) Repo-root executable shadowing: resolveCandidate falls back to join(root, candidate.command) and spawns it with cwd=root, env=process.env, no timeout (src/audit/orchestrator/localCommands.ts:98-126), so a repo shipping an executable named prettier/black/gofmt/python/npx at its root gets it run when the real tool is off PATH. (c) The default-deny allowlist is bypassable by path prefix: executableBaseName strips directories via split('/').pop() (src/shared/tooling/allowlistedExec.ts:214-223), so argv ['src/grep','-n','x'] base-names to grep, passes, and spawns with cwd = repo root. (d) Ecosystem runners execute repo build code by design (npx -y, pipx run, cargo, bundle exec at acquisitionEngine.ts:172-183,350) with nothing pinning --no-install/--offline/--locked and no timeout or output cap. (e) LLM-authored command strings reach a shell: test_command/e2e_command are accepted behind only a typeof string check (src/remediate/steps/nextStep.ts:1638-1641) then spawnSync(..., {shell:true}) (src/remediate/phases/close.ts:885-890, :996-1001), as are targeted_commands sourced from the audit report (worktreeLifecycle.ts:257-262); the filters are heuristic DENYLISTS with no executable allowlist. These are the only three shell:true sites in src/ and all three carry non-tool-authored strings. (f) Blast radius is amplified because the env scrub removes only CLAUDECODE, /^CLAUDE_CODE/ and AUDIT_TOOLS_CALLER_CWD (src/shared/tooling/exec.ts:306-320), so every provider API key and GITHUB_TOKEN is inherited by every child. What makes this design rather than a bug list is where the boundary WAS drawn: the path reaching the NETWORK is rigorous (fixed vendor URLs, sha256 verification, an admitSpawn chokepoint, only gitleaks admitted by default) while the paths reaching the untrusted input itself have no gate — admitSpawn cannot help with (a) because that is import(), not spawn, and consent_token is an existence check rather than an authorization (any non-blank string admits every non-default candidate, acquisitionEngine.ts:216-225). Fix as a class: resolve analyzer dependencies from the shared version-keyed cache or the tool's own install and NEVER from the audited tree (read a needed version from the manifest and installToCache it); drop the repo-root fallback in resolveCandidate; base-name only after rejecting any token containing a path separator; route the three shell:true sites through argv plus the existing allowlist so a model-supplied command is authorized rather than merely un-denylisted; scrub the child env to a declared passlist. Then write down the threat model — a repo-wide grep for 'threat model' returns nothing, and a tool whose purpose is pointing at code you have reason to distrust needs a stated answer to what the audited repo is allowed to do to us. The answer is already written for downloaded binaries.

findings.title: Nothing pins the revision under audit, so the continuity model silently assumes a frozen tree and punishes the long runs it was built for
findings.summary: Raised independently by two perspectives (pragmatist, adversary) with non-overlapping evidence, which is the strongest corroboration in the review. The load-bearing unexamined assumption of the whole artifact model is that the audited tree does not change during a run; nothing enforces or even records it. There is no run-level revision pin anywhere in the audit half — no pinned_revision/git_sha/head_sha/snapshotSha field in src/shared/types/sessionConfig.ts, src/audit/types/auditScope.ts, or the run ledger — so every extraction reads the live working tree. Drift IS detected: checkFileIntegrity re-hashes a task's files against recorded manifest hashes (src/audit/orchestrator/fileIntegrity.ts:19-62). The handling is the most expensive available: on !integrity.is_clean, nextStepHelpers.ts:2646-2658 re-runs intake, which re-extracts repo_manifest, whose content hash changes, which cascades the staleness DAG through the planning chain (repo_manifest is a declared input to audit_tasks.json, charter_register.json and coverage_matrix.json per spec/audit/dependency-map.md:37-107). The project's own records confirm the observed consequence: docs/HANDOFF.md instructs laps to land work WITHOUT a run because a commit mid-run re-stales the planning chain and regresses it to charter_extraction, and docs/backlog/open-bugs.md:511 records a real 313-packet run invalidated exactly that way. This is the expected case, not an edge: every property the design is proud of pushes runs toward being LONG (bounded per-invocation steps, resumability across sessions, quota pacing that deliberately waits for windows to reset, cooperative peers). Secondary cost: cross-wave incommensurability — wave 1 and wave 2 can review different trees and their findings merge as if describing one codebase — and A9 (peers joining one run) is incoherent without an agreed answer to which tree the run is about. This is also the mechanical reason the project has no clean validation evidence (see DR-003): developing the tool and validating it on itself are mutually exclusive. Stated precisely so it is not overclaimed: the citation half is already largely defended, because quote grounding matches on CONTENT not line numbers (src/shared/validation/findingGrounding.ts:158-193), so findings survive line shifts. The machinery for the fix also already exists with the wrong lifetime: createReviewSnapshot does git worktree add --detach HEAD (src/shared/providers/reviewSnapshot.ts:104) but is torn down per drive, and src/remediate/steps/dispatch/worktreeLifecycle.ts is a 900-line worktree substrate that already adds at HEAD and copies gitignored files over. Capture one revision at run start, record it in the run ledger as the run's identity, and resolve every read through it. A moved HEAD then becomes an explicit operator decision (continue against the pinned revision, or re-baseline) instead of an invisible staleness cascade. This is the cheapest-now/expensive-later item in the review: retrofitting later means re-basing the provenance of every artifact hash and every anchor. Non-git targets keep today's behavior.

findings.title: (judge-added) The standing decision that effort and complexity are not costs removed the only brake on the accretion this entire review is measuring
findings.summary: No perspective questioned this, and it is the generative cause behind a large fraction of what all five independently found. docs/project-philosophy.md:74 and :245 state, as a standing preference, that effort, complexity and refactor size are NOT costs — only the eventual endpoint matters — and CLAUDE.md repeats it with the instruction never to defer or pick a lighter half-measure because the ideal is a lot of work. That rule is correct as an answer to the question it was written for (do not ship a half-measure to save labor). But it was generalized into a claim about complexity itself, and complexity is a cost that is paid by every future reader and every future mechanism, not by the author at the moment of the change. With that cost declared to be zero, nothing in the project's decision procedure ever argues against adding a mechanism. The aggregate result is measurable and is what the other 44 findings describe from five different angles: 23 verify legs of which 11 police the project's own prose (DR-018), ~17,500 lines of enforcement machinery outside any typechecker (DR-019), 26 parity/drift tests standing in for extraction the project's own rule prefers (DR-023), 13 hooks, a guard-reach registry, a doc manifest, an attestation system, four separate drain ceilings, five hand-authored materializations of one obligation relation (DR-010), ~179,300 lines of tests against ~143,700 lines of source, and a 1.29 MB deliverable nobody can read (DR-012) — for a tool with two commands and one user. Note the asymmetry the short-attention perspective isolated independently: the parts a USER touches (step prompts, step contracts, the report's first 90 lines) are consistently well-budgeted, while the parts only a MAINTAINER touches are consistently not. That is exactly what a zero-cost-complexity rule predicts, because a user-facing budget has an external forcing function and an internal one has none. The project already proves it can price complexity when it decides to: check:backlog-budget exists precisely because backlog entries grew past navigability, and MAX_DRAIN_STEPS, DEFAULT_SCOPE_MAX_FILES and the packet budget cap are all deliberate ceilings on the product's own behavior. Recommendation, framed as a decision for the owner rather than a defect: narrow the rule to what it was for — do not trade the correct endpoint for less labor — and restore complexity as a real cost in the design gate, so that 'this adds a mechanism a future reader must hold' counts against a change, and 'this deletes one' counts for it. Concretely, extend the /design-check gate to require that a change proposing a new mechanism name what it deletes, and point the existing budget-gate mechanism at the internal surfaces (CLAUDE.md, the gate roster, the hook roster) that currently have no ceiling. Without this, every recommendation in this review that says 'add a mechanism' makes the problem worse, and every one that says 'delete two and derive the third' will keep losing to the rule as written.

findings.title: (judge-added) What the tool calls verification proves only that a quoted span exists; the tier that could establish falsity never fired, and 61 grounded verdicts carry no quote at all
findings.summary: Every perspective either credited quote-grounding as the North Star correctly implemented (adversary, explicitly) or complained about how it is TALLIED (pragmatist, DR-006). None asked what the property actually establishes, and the answer changes how much of the product's trust claim survives. Grounding is defined in src/shared/validation/findingGrounding.ts: a finding is grounded as soon as ONE of its affected_files[].quoted_text spans re-reads from its cited file, content-matched with whitespace/CRLF normalization (:158-193). That proves the cited code EXISTS. It does not evaluate the claim made about the code. The schema carries a second, stronger tier — status refuted means an executable anchor DISPROVED the claim (src/shared/types/finding.ts:57,63) — and that is the only mechanism in the pipeline that can establish a finding is false. On the committed 1480-finding self-audit it fired zero times: 0 refuted, and 0 findings carry any runtime_validation or anchor field at all (verified by direct scan of .audit-tools/audit-findings.json; summary.runtime_validation_status_breakdown is absent). So in practice 'verified' means 'the quote exists', while README.md:85-86 says 'adversarially verified' and the README's own illustrative sample advertises a verdict vocabulary the contract has no field for (186 verified-real of 204 extracted, 10 false, 8 uncertain). Second, the weak property is not even internally consistent in the shipped artifact: 61 of the 436 findings marked grounded carry no non-empty quoted_text on any affected_files entry (386 of 1480 findings carry a quote at all), which the module's own stated rule says must be ungrounded — a finding that carries no quote at all is ungrounded. Either those verdicts are wrong, or the evidence backing them was discarded when the contract was written; both are defects, and nothing checks either. Why this is the deeper half of DR-006: fixing the tally so the counts sum to 1480 makes the report honest about HOW MANY findings were checked, while leaving the reader to believe that a checked finding was assessed for truth. Recommendation: (1) add a contract invariant, enforced at ingest and in the validator rather than by a producer, that status==='grounded' requires either a re-verifiable quote present in the persisted record or an anchor verdict — so the 61 cannot exist; (2) rename the reported bucket to what it measures (citation_verified) and state in the render that it is an existence check, not a truth check; (3) treat the A2 oracle corpus (docs/backlog/forward-tracks.md:108-126, which already reasons correctly that labeling only what the tool FOUND measures precision while recall needs ground truth the tool did not author) as the only instrument that can measure the property the product actually claims, and gate release on it. Until something measures finding precision, the whole verification apparatus is optimizing a proxy — and DR-013's 1138 maintainability findings versus 1 security finding is what an unmeasured proxy looks like from outside.

findings.title: Anchor allowlist pins the executable NAME, not the binary: a repo-local `grep.cmd` is admitted and run through cmd.exe with cwd set to the audited repo
findings.summary:
INFERRED CONTRACT: two explicit safety claims. (1) only "inspection-only executables" may run — `isAllowedAnchorCommand` is "the single authority for what the tool will auto-run on the model's behalf" (src/shared/tooling/allowlistedExec.ts:286-294); (2) commands "run only via `runAllowlistedReadOnlyCommand`, which spawns argv-only (never a shell)" (allowlistedExec.ts:22-24, repeated at :322-324). The module was hardened once already against CVE-2024-27980, so the threat model is acknowledged.

COUNTEREXAMPLE: the allowlist validates a *derived name* while the runner spawns the *caller's original string*. `executableBaseName` strips any directory and then strips a `.cmd`/`.bat`/`.exe` suffix (allowlistedExec.ts:215-223); `isAllowedAnchorCommand` matches that basename (:298-303); but `runAllowlistedReadOnlyCommand` spawns `resolveExecArgv(command)` built from the untouched `command[0]` (:339-340). Verified by running the shipped code:
  `["./grep.cmd","x","."]`             → allowed: true → spawns `["C:\\Windows\\system32\\cmd.exe","/d","/s","/c","./grep.cmd x ."]`
  `["grep.bat","x"]`                   → allowed: true → spawns via cmd.exe
  `["C:/tmp/evil/git.exe","log"]`      → allowed: true → spawns that exact binary
  `["tools/rg","x"]`                   → allowed: true → spawns `tools/rg`
So BOTH claims fail. The identity claim fails because any path whose last segment matches after suffix-stripping is admitted — the allowlist constrains what the file is *called*, not what it is. The "never a shell" claim fails on win32 because `resolveExecArgv` → `wrapForWindowsBatch` (src/shared/tooling/exec.ts:238-248) routes any `.cmd`/`.bat` through `cmd.exe /d /s /c`, which is a command interpreter. (The `quoteForCmd` hardening is sound and does neutralize metacharacter injection — the gap here is executable identity and the shell hop, not quoting.)

WHY IT MATTERS: `runAllowlistedReadOnlyCommand` is called with `cwd = repoRoot` (anchorGrounding.ts:178), i.e. the repository being audited, and audit-code's purpose is auditing codebases it does not own. cmd.exe resolves a relative command against its own cwd, so `./grep.cmd` denotes a file in the *untrusted* repository. A repo containing a `grep.cmd`/`git.bat` plus an anchor naming it therefore executes repo-supplied code at ingest, with only the `CLAUDE_CODE*` env stripped. The existing `admitSpawn` consent gate shows the project already treats repo-triggered subprocess execution as requiring consent; this path has no such gate. Note the test suite explicitly blesses a path-shaped executable (`["/usr/bin/grep","x"]` at tests/shared/allowlisted-exec.test.ts:64 / tests/audit/anchor-grounding.test.ts:64) and no test covers a `.cmd`/`.bat`/relative-path form, so the gap is uncovered rather than known-accepted.

RECOMMENDED CHANGE: require `command[0]` to be a bare token (no `/`, `\`, or drive letter) and to match an allowlisted name with NO suffix stripping; resolve it to an absolute path yourself against a trusted PATH and spawn that resolved path. Refuse a `.cmd`/`.bat` target outright rather than wrapping it, so the "never a shell" invariant holds on win32 too. Add the adversarial cases above as refusal tests beside the existing ones.

findings.title: audit-tools/shared is a single flat barrel of 1,041 re-exports, so the shared core has no internal boundaries — and quota-to-providers is a real runtime import cycle nobody can see
findings.summary: Two perspectives found this independently; the mathematician's evidence is decisive because it names a concrete violation the barrel conceals. src/shared/index.ts is 1,531 lines re-exporting 1,041 named symbols across 277 export blocks, and it is the only realistic way to consume the shared area: 587 import sites use the barrel, only 10 use the shared/* subpath package.json already publishes, and tests reach past both with 322 deep-relative ../../src/shared/... imports — three coexisting idioms for one dependency, with the same module imported both ways (tests/audit/quota-file-lock.test.ts uses the subpath while tests/remediate/quota-file-lock.test.ts imports the same functions from the barrel). Two concrete consequences. First, the barrel has become a maintained artifact with its own drift test: tests/shared/shared-tests-invariants.test.mjs contains seven assertions (INV-shared-tests-07) whose entire content is that named symbols still appear in the barrel. A test pinning the membership of an index is a sign the index is doing work a module boundary should do. Second, and worse, the layering is unobservable and is in fact violated: src/shared/quota/apiPool.ts:28 value-imports from src/shared/providers/sharedProviderConfirmation.ts, which at line 65 value-imports gatherDispatchableSources back from ../quota/apiPool.js — a genuine runtime cycle between the quota and providers layers, with providers/identity.ts closing a third. There is no answer to whether quota depends on providers or the reverse because both are true, and no consumer of the barrel could notice, since everything arrives from one namespace. It also defeats the review affordances the project relies on elsewhere: the single import statement at src/remediate/steps/nextStep.ts:13 is 1,857 characters pulling roughly 100 symbols in one line, which is not diffable, so a change in what a module depends on is invisible in review. Recommendation: make the published subpaths the real interface (audit-tools/shared/quota, /providers, /dispatch, /io, /graph, /reporting), each a small deliberate surface; keep the root barrel for external consumers only; add a check: leg forbidding root-barrel imports inside src/; and let the resulting import errors expose the actual dependency order, forcing the quota/providers cycle to be resolved (extract the shared identity/pool-key vocabulary both need into a leaf module) rather than merely reported. That converts the layering from an unstated intention into a checked property and deletes INV-shared-tests-07 as unrepresentable. Note DR-029: the repo's own cycle guard cannot see this cycle either, for the same reason.

findings.title: Eleven of twenty-three release-gate legs validate the project's own prose, not the shipped product
findings.summary: Two perspectives counted this independently and I re-verified the leg list from package.json: verify:checks has exactly 23 legs, of which eleven exist solely to police the repository's own markdown, backlog and memory index — check:constitutional-doc-paths, check:doc-manifest, check:doc-links, check:doc-code-citations, check:philosophy-brief, check:nightly-routine-prompt, check:handoff-roadmap, check:backlog-index, check:memory-citations, check:backlog-budget, check:backlog-status. Three more (check:control-bytes, check:guard-reach, check:loop-core-patterns) police repo and hook hygiene, leaving eight legs actually exercising what ships. Measured: those governance scripts total ~3,498 lines against ~749 lines for the product gates (verify:hosts, verify:remediate-hosts, pack:smoke and the two packaged smokes). On top sit 3,010 lines across 13 hooks in .claude/hooks/, ~1,084 lines of nightly-review machinery in scripts/nightly/, a 35.8 KB CLAUDE.md, and 19,105 lines of markdown across 95 docs. Resolving the disagreement between perspectives on cost: the wall-clock price is genuinely negligible — the eleven doc gates account for roughly 4.5s of a 96-241s verify:checks run per .audit-tools-profile/verify-checks-history.ndjson — which is precisely why this is a design finding rather than a performance one. The real price is maintenance and comprehension: every one is a bespoke parser with its own failure modes and its own escape hatches, and each is something a contributor or agent must hold in working memory before touching a doc. The generative cause is applying the product's rule A3 (whatever can be enforced in tooling must be) to the development process, where the payoff is far smaller and the surface is unbounded prose — see DR-004 for why nothing counterbalanced it. Recommendation: collapse the eleven into one doc-lint entrypoint over a single declarative manifest, and delete the generated-prose round-trips (check:philosophy-brief, check:handoff-roadmap, check:backlog-index) in favor of generating those artifacts at release time without a drift gate — a generator plus a gate checking the generator is two mechanisms where one suffices.

findings.title: Executable-anchor "confirmed" verdict is self-certifying: the model authors both the command and its success predicate
findings.summary:
INFERRED CONTRACT: `anchorGrounding.ts` states it plainly — "the confirmed bit is the tool's run — never the model's word" (src/audit/validation/anchorGrounding.ts:9-10). The tier-2 anchor pass exists precisely because tier-1 cannot verify a *behavior* claim, and the docstring cites real hallucinated findings (a fabricated dependency cycle) that only a deterministic re-run caught.

COUNTEREXAMPLE: the finding supplies BOTH halves of the experiment. `finding.executable_anchor.command` is model-authored AND `finding.executable_anchor.confirm_if` — the predicate that decides confirmed-vs-refuted — is also model-authored. Nothing anywhere relates the command to the claim. So the model can pick any command/predicate pair that is true by construction. Verified by running the shipped code: `isAllowedAnchorCommand(["git","log","-1"])` → true, and `confirm_if: {kind: "exit_zero"}` makes `evaluateExpectation` (anchorGrounding.ts:116-120) return `confirmed: true` on any repo with a commit. `["git","rev-parse","HEAD"]` and `["git","status"]` are likewise admitted and likewise always exit 0. The `output_excludes` kind is even cheaper: any text unlikely to appear in the output confirms.

AMPLIFIER: `combineGroundingWithAnchor` (anchorGrounding.ts:226) promotes a confirmed anchor to `{status: "grounded"}` UNCONDITIONALLY, discarding the tier-1 verdict — verified: `combineGroundingWithAnchor({status:"ungrounded",reason:"quote not found on disk"}, {status:"confirmed"})` returns `{"status":"grounded"}`. So a self-confirming anchor LAUNDERS a finding whose cited code does not exist from `ungrounded` into `grounded`. The consequence is not cosmetic: `findingIsGrounded` (src/shared/validation/findingGrounding.ts:207) is what the remediator consults, and `groundingVerificationBullet` (src/remediate/steps/dispatch/implementPrompt.ts:328) returns an empty string for a grounded finding — so the "VERIFY BEFORE FIX" instruction is suppressed and a remediation worker applies a fix to a fabricated claim without re-checking. This inverts INV-GND-02, whose whole point is that a missing verdict must never be mistaken for a passing one.

RECOMMENDED CHANGE: treat a model-chosen predicate as untrusted. Either (a) restrict `confirm_if` to kinds the tool derives from the claim rather than the model (e.g. the anchor must reference the finding's own cited path/symbol, and `exit_zero` on a command with no relation to the claim is refused), or (b) stop letting an anchor OVERRIDE a failed tier-1: make `grounded` require tier-1 to pass, and let a confirming anchor only ADD evidence. Option (b) is the smaller change and restores the invariant that the tool's own re-read is the floor. At minimum, record the anchor verdict as a separate field rather than collapsing it into `grounding.status`, so a downstream consumer can tell "quote re-verified" from "the model's own predicate passed".

findings.title: git anchor validation misses exec-capable flags on read-only subcommands: `git grep -O<pager>` / `--open-files-in-pager` executes an arbitrary program
findings.summary: The module's stated posture is default-deny ('New dangerous flags are therefore refused by construction'), but git is validated with a DENYLIST (GIT_REFUSED_OPTIONS) plus a read-only-subcommand check. git grep's `-O` / `--open-files-in-pager[=<cmd>]` runs the named program on the matching files, is not in GIT_REFUSED_OPTIONS, and `grep` is an allowed read-only subcommand — so isAllowedAnchorCommand(["git","grep","-O","sh","pattern"]) returns true and the model-authored anchor executes an arbitrary command at ingest, the exact CRIT ARC-a06a3945 class this module exists to refuse. Related exec-capable flags on allowed subcommands (e.g. `--ext-diff`/`--textconv` on diff/log/show, which run repo-config-defined external commands) are also unrefused, though those need a config vector.
evidence: src/shared/tooling/allowlistedExec.ts:195-203 - GIT_REFUSED_OPTIONS does not contain -O or --open-files-in-pager, git-grep's run-a-program flag

src/shared/tooling/allowlistedExec.ts:272-283 - isAllowedGitCommand refuses only denylisted flag names; every other flag on a read-only subcommand passes, so git is denylist-posture while every other executable is default-deny
src/shared/tooling/allowlistedExec.ts:177-187 - 'grep' is in GIT_READONLY_SUBCOMMANDS, so the whole command is admitted and would be spawned by runAllowlistedReadOnlyCommand

findings.title: Git option denylist bypass via attached short flags in isAllowedGitCommand
findings.summary: isAllowedGitCommand uses GIT_REFUSED_OPTIONS.has(flagName(arg)) to refuse dangerous git options, but flagName does not separate attached short flag values like -ccore.pager=cmd or -ofile. Consequently, git commands with attached short options bypass refusal checks, allowing arbitrary code execution or file writes.

findings.title: No gate enforces artifact-registry ⊆ dependency-DAG: an artifact can be registered with no DAG node and silently never participate in staleness propagation
findings.summary:
INFERRED CONTRACT: "Artifacts are continuity; dependency DAG is truth. Staleness propagates along an explicit dependency map — never ad-hoc freshness checks" (CLAUDE.md). For that to hold, every artifact in the authoritative registry (`ARTIFACT_DEFINITIONS`, src/audit/io/artifacts.ts) must be a node in `ARTIFACT_DEPENDS_ON_MAP` (src/audit/orchestrator/dependencyMap.ts:40) — otherwise it is invisible to `computeStaleArtifacts` and neither stales nor is staled.

COUNTEREXAMPLE: the existing gates check only ONE direction. INV-11 (tests/audit/audit-orchestrator-invariants.test.ts:597-621) and the PARITY tests (tests/audit/seam-dependency-map-executor-writeset-parity.test.ts:261-303) all assert map ⊆ registry — that every DAG node is a known artifact. Nothing asserts the converse. Verified by computing the set difference from the built code: the registry has 38 entries, the DAG 35 nodes, and four registry artifacts are NOT DAG nodes — `artifact_metadata.json`, `audit_state.json`, `auto_fixes_applied.json`, `provider_confirmation.json`. Only the first is a documented, structurally-deliberate exclusion (the metadata file cannot depend on itself, and it is filtered out explicitly at artifactMetadata.ts:95-99 and staleness.ts:94); the other three carry no exclusion note anywhere. Also verified: `ALL_DAG_ARTIFACTS` — the set that would make such a check trivial — is imported by exactly two source files and by ZERO tests or scripts, and nothing under `scripts/` touches the dependency map at all. So the correspondence is unguarded in the direction that matters, and a newly registered artifact gets no DAG node and no failing build.

MOST CONSEQUENTIAL INSTANCE: `auto_fixes_applied.json` records the auto-fix executor's work, and that executor REWRITES SOURCE FILES in the audited tree (`prettier --write` and friends, src/audit/orchestrator/autoFixExecutor.ts:157-166). Neither that marker nor `repo_manifest.json` declares an edge, so the DAG has no representation of "the tree was mutated after extraction". Source drift is caught by separate content-key/file-integrity mechanisms rather than by the DAG, which is itself in tension with the "never ad-hoc freshness checks" half of the contract.

RECOMMENDED CHANGE: add the missing direction as a contract test (and, given the repo's `check:guard-reach` posture, register it): assert `registry ⊆ ALL_DAG_ARTIFACTS` with an explicit, named allowlist of deliberate exclusions carrying the reason as data — so `artifact_metadata.json` passes with its rationale recorded and the other three must either gain a DAG node or gain an explicit exclusion entry. Separately, decide `auto_fixes_applied.json` on its merits: if an auto-fix invalidates extraction, give it a real edge into `repo_manifest.json` rather than leaving the invalidation to a parallel mechanism.

findings.title: One lens produced 77% of the findings and security produced exactly one; nothing budgets per-lens yield or rolls up N instances of one pattern
findings.summary: Two perspectives converged and I re-verified the breakdown directly from .audit-tools/audit-findings.json: of 1480 findings, maintainability 1138, correctness 103, tests 92, architecture 44, observability 39, reliability 23, operability 13, data_integrity 11, config_deployment 8, performance 8, security 1. One lens is 77% of the deliverable, and 1133 of those 1138 are medium or low, consuming the majority of all finding prose. Security producing a single finding is not credible for a codebase that spawns subprocesses, imports code from the audited tree, admits external analyzer binaries, writes into user worktrees and shells out to gh — DR-001 alone is a security finding class with six instances that the security lens did not surface, which is direct evidence that the lens under-fires rather than that the code is clean. Every admission gate in the pipeline is per-finding — grounding, adversarial confirmation, dedup — so there is no per-lens yield ceiling and no aggregation step that turns 'this pattern appears in 400 files' into one finding with 400 sites. A lens whose nature is to emit roughly one observation per file mechanically swamps everything else, and the 78 high-severity findings the executive summary is actually about are 5% of the artifact they are buried in. Average summary length is 283 characters, so this is a thousand short entries rather than a few long ones. The consequence is not only readability: remediate-code consumes this same contract, so the imbalance propagates into planning and dispatch, and work is sized by a finding count one lens dominates. And the summary reports the imbalance as a neutral count line, so a lens returning 1 finding and a lens returning 1,138 are presented identically with nothing marking either as anomalous. Recommendation: add a per-lens rollup obligation before synthesis that collapses N instances of one pattern into a single finding carrying N sites, and surface per-lens yield against an expected band in the summary so a runaway or silent lens is visible in the report rather than only in its line count. This also directly relieves DR-013, since most of the 17,941 report lines are this one lens. The 77% share additionally deserves a product decision: that lens generates the bulk of the artifact and almost none of the top risks.

findings.title: One relation (obligation id to order, executor, runner, execute) is hand-materialized in four tables on the audit side and inlined in a 5,506-line monolith on the remediate side
findings.summary: Two perspectives found opposite-looking things about the same relation and both are correct at different granularity — that resolution is the finding. The mathematician's view: the audit obligation layer has one primitive concept (an ordered set of named obligations, each with a way to satisfy it) written down five times, four by hand — PRIORITY (27 ids, hand-ordered, src/audit/orchestrator/nextStep.ts:25), EXECUTOR_REGISTRY (src/audit/orchestrator/executors.ts:18), EXECUTOR_RUNNERS (executorRunners.ts), buildAuditObligations() (src/audit/cli/nextStepHelpers.ts:1921) — and the fifth, buildDrainObligations() at advance.ts:441, is PRIORITY.map(...), i.e. derived. The cost of the four copies is visible as three separate consistency mechanisms: a load-time throw (assertExecutorRegistryCoversPriority, nextStep.ts:70), tests/audit/executor-registry-sync.test.ts reconciling three of them, and tests/audit/priority-chain-invariants.test.ts restating the relative order a third time as an assertion list. The sync test's own comment records a defect that already escaped through this multiplicity: an id present in PRIORITY but absent from buildAuditObligations() was silently skipped on the primary path (the dropped structure_decomposition_current obligation, doc-review D-56). Critically, the one representation that is computed rather than typed is the only one no test has to guard — the codebase already carries the proof that derivation works here. The short-attention view, verified: src/audit/orchestrator/nextStep.ts is 186 lines and src/audit/orchestrator/executors.ts is 193, so audit's control flow is ~380 lines of readable data; src/remediate/steps/nextStep.ts is 5,506 lines with 86 top-level functions and 27 exports, where the two ladders (PRE_INTAKE_PRIORITY at 4830, MAIN_PRIORITY at 5040) are perfectly legible on their own but sit inside a file that also holds intake gates, the review gate, ambiguity gate, phase-boundary gate, rolling dispatch drivers, clarification/triage appliers and both obligation builders — buildImplementDispatchStep alone spans lines 1869-2564. So audit's FILE is the model to copy while audit's RELATION is itself duplicated four ways; the two observations do not conflict. Combined recommendation, and it is mechanical rather than a redesign because both halves of the target already exist in this repo: define one table of obligation records ({id, executor, kind, runner, dependsOn}) as the shared vocabulary both modes instantiate, with everything else a projection — PRIORITY a topological sort over dependsOn (see DR-023), the registry a groupBy(executor), the CLI/orchestrator obligation arrays a map. Extract remediate's obligations into that registry and move each handler to its own module so src/remediate/steps/nextStep.ts ends up around 200 lines. assertExecutorRegistryCoversPriority, executor-registry-sync.test.ts and priority-chain-invariants.test.ts then become unrepresentable rather than enforced, because a record cannot be missing a field its type requires. If only one structural change is made, this is the highest-leverage one available: it removes four hand-maintained tables, three consistency mechanisms, the entire class of defect D-56 belongs to, and the largest single block of cognitive load in the repo.

findings.title: Quote-and-verify grounding admits any non-empty span, so a one-character quote grounds any fabricated finding
findings.summary:
INFERRED CONTRACT: the S7 anti-hallucination gate. "every finding cites a verbatim span (`affected_files[].quoted_text`); the tool re-reads that span from disk and content-matches it... a quote naming code that does not exist cannot match" (src/shared/validation/findingGrounding.ts:5-13). The safeguard is explicitly "attached to the *claim*".

COUNTEREXAMPLE: the only threshold on the cited span is non-blankness — `typeof loc.quoted_text === "string" && loc.quoted_text.trim().length > 0` (findingGrounding.ts:169) — and the match is a substring test over whitespace-collapsed text (`quoteMatches`, findingGrounding.ts:144-148). There is no minimum length, no distinctiveness/entropy requirement, and no check that the span is anywhere near the finding's claimed `line_start`/`line_end`. Grepped the whole tree: no `MIN_QUOTE`/quote-length constant exists anywhere. Verified by running the shipped code against a real repo file: `quoted_text` of `"}"`, `";"`, `"import"`, and `"  return  "` each returned `{"status":"grounded"}`. Every one of those substrings appears in essentially every source file in the repo, so the gate is satisfiable without reading the file at all.

WHY IT MATTERS: this makes `grounded` carry close to zero evidential weight while the report and the remediator both treat it as the confirmed state. `synthesis.ts:465` tells the reader that ungrounded findings are "not confirmed — treat them with skepticism", which by contrast asserts that grounded findings ARE confirmed; and as in DR-001, `grounded` suppresses the remediator's VERIFY-BEFORE-FIX bullet. A weak or adversarial worker that emits plausible-sounding findings with a `}` quote gets them all marked confirmed and fixed unverified. Note this defeats the gate in the *opposite* direction from the one the design worried about: the docstring reasons carefully about false NEGATIVES (line shifts must not false-fail a valid quote) and not at all about false POSITIVES.

RECOMMENDED CHANGE: require the cited span to be evidence rather than merely present. Concretely: enforce a minimum normalized length (a span shorter than ~30 normalized chars or fewer than ~3 tokens grounds nothing), require the match to be reasonably unique in the file (reject a needle occurring more than N times), and — since `line_start`/`line_end` are already validated against `file_coverage` — require the matched offset to fall inside the finding's own cited span rather than anywhere in the file. All three are mechanical and cheap, and they keep the deliberate whitespace/CRLF tolerance intact.

findings.title: Rerun after a completed audit never promotes its new report: alreadyPromoted check mistakes a prior run's promoted file for this run's promotion
findings.summary: promoteIfFrictionSatisfied treats the mere existence of the parent .audit-tools/audit-report.md as 'this run already promoted' and returns early. promoteFinalAuditReport deletes only artifactsDir and leaves the promoted pair in the parent dir (remediate consumes it there; nothing ever deletes it), so a second audit run — the rerun the module's own docstring says the cleanup exists to enable — reaches completion, finds the previous run's promoted file, skips promotion forever, never cleans artifactsDir, and surfaces the PREVIOUS audit's stale report as this run's finalReportPath. The headless path (advanceAuditCommand.ts) promotes unconditionally on complete and thus overwrites correctly; only this conversation-first path has the guard.

affected_files.quoted_text: const alreadyPromoted = await access(promotedPath).then(() => true).catch(() => false);

evidence: src/audit/cli/nextStepHelpers.ts:377-379 - the guard's only evidence of 'already promoted' is access() on the parent-dir file, which persists across audit runs.

src/audit/io/artifacts.ts:427-473 - promoteFinalAuditReport copies to dirname(artifactsDir) and removes only artifactsDir; the promoted audit-report.md/audit-findings.json in the parent are never deleted by any later code path (grep over src/ finds no unlink/rm of promotedAuditReportPath).

src/audit/cli/advanceAuditCommand.ts:68-70,104-106 - the headless complete path calls promoteFinalAuditReport unconditionally (no alreadyPromoted guard), so the two completion paths disagree on rerun behavior.

findings.title: Reviewer independence — the project's own anti-self-grading conviction — is enforced only as prompt text, and tested only as prompt text
findings.summary: Do not grade your own homework — anything important gets an independent adversarial check that is allowed to refuse — is one of the project's headline convictions, and independence is the property the entire adversarial layer's value rests on. It is currently guaranteed by asking the host politely. renderIndependentReviewerDirective (src/audit/orchestrator/designReviewPrompt.ts:202-219) emits prose: the host MUST dispatch this review to a fresh, independent sub-agent that did not author the work, and must NOT perform the review inline. Nothing verifies it happened. There is no reviewer identity on a review result, no session or provider provenance recorded for a review, and no refusal path when the reviewing context is the authoring context — searching reviewer_id / reviewed_by / author_session across src/audit, src/remediate and src/shared finds provenance fields for charters, capabilities and analyzers, but none for who performed a review. The test makes the gap unusually visible because it tests the request rather than the outcome: tests/audit/mandatory-independent-critic.test.ts:28-46 asserts the prompt STRING matches /Independent review — MANDATORY/ and /MUST dispatch/. A green suite proves the tool asked, not that anyone complied. The FreshSessionProvider contract (src/shared/providers/types.ts:143-153) offers launch and nothing about identity, so even the provider layer cannot express 'this reviewer differs from that author'. The degraded branch is honest about running inline when the host reports it cannot dispatch (:217-219), but that capability flag is host-asserted too, so a host can select its own degradation. This is A3 inverted at the one place it matters most: everywhere else audit-tools refuses to trust the host (a finding must carry a verbatim span the tool re-reads from disk, and the confirmed bit is the tool's re-check, never the model's word), and that pattern is absent one layer up where the question shifts from 'is this finding real' to 'was this judgment independent'. A capable host complies; a weak one self-reviews and produces output indistinguishable from the real thing — precisely the failure the North Star exists to rule out. Recommendation: have the dispatch substrate, not the prompt, stamp each review artifact with the identity of the session/provider that produced it, and have ingest refuse or downgrade to a surfaced self_reviewed verdict — exactly as ungrounded is surfaced — when a review's producer identity matches the authoring producer or is absent. The parallel-perspective fan-out already writes each reviewer's findings to a separate file, so the seam where identity could be stamped already exists. Independence then degrades visibly instead of silently, which is all the North Star requires.

findings.title: SARIF — the OASIS standard for static-analysis interchange — is ignored in favor of eleven hand-written per-tool JSON parsers, and half the adapter directory is already dead
findings.summary: The acquire-and-normalize strategy is right, but it normalizes at the wrong layer. src/audit/extractors/analyzers/candidates.ts (848 lines) declares 11 external tools, each with a bespoke parse function reading that tool's proprietary JSON: gitleaks, semgrep, eslint, knip, jscpd, osv-scanner, clippy (NDJSON), rubocop, hadolint, actionlint, type-coverage. Every one of semgrep, ESLint, clippy, hadolint, actionlint and osv-scanner can emit SARIF instead, and CodeQL emits it by default. SARIF already carries exactly the fields ExternalAnalyzerResultItemSchema defines in src/audit/types/externalAnalyzer.ts — rule id, level, message, artifact URI, region start/end line — plus a tool.driver.rules table with descriptions and help URIs the current parsers throw away. Normalizing on SARIF collapses eleven parsers into one, after which every future SARIF-emitting analyzer needs only a buildArgv and a detect, with no parser at all. The cost of the current shape is already visible as decay: src/audit/adapters/ contains nine adapters (795 lines) of which only clippy.ts and rubocop.ts have any importer under src/ — semgrep.ts, eslint.ts, astGrep.ts, codeql.ts, npmAudit.ts and coverageSummary.ts are reachable only from tests, while candidates.ts carries its own independent second implementations of the semgrep and ESLint parsers. src/audit/adapters/codeql.ts is the one file that reads SARIF, via ~20 lines of hand-written partial interfaces, and it consumes only codeFlows/threadFlows — discarding results[].message, level, locations, ruleIndex and the rules table, so CodeQL findings are dropped and only source-to-sink file edges survive. There is no sarif type package, no schema validation of SARIF input, and no mention of the format anywhere in docs/ or spec/. Recommendation: make SARIF the acquisition contract — request the SARIF output format where the tool supports it, validate against the published SARIF 2.1.0 schema, map SARIF to the internal item shape once, keep bespoke parsers only for tools that genuinely cannot emit it (npm audit, type-coverage, jscpd), and delete the unreferenced adapters plus the duplicate semgrep/eslint parsers in the same change.

findings.title: The commit gate is at the wrong seam: a 1,172-line vendor agent hook with a 519-line function, binding for no human, no fresh clone, and none of the other agent hosts this project ships support for
findings.summary: Two perspectives found the same file for different reasons (novelty-seeker: wrong seam; short-attention: unreadable), and the fixes converge, so they are one finding. The project's loudest invariant is that correctness properties are guaranteed by tooling rather than a host remembering, and that host/IDE is never baked in; the commit gate violates both. .claude/hooks/pre-commit-gate.mjs (1,172 lines / 58 KB, with runGate spanning lines 427-946 — a single 519-line function) is registered in .claude/settings.json as a Claude Code PreToolUse hook matching Bash|PowerShell. It is not a git hook: git ls-files finds no tracked hooks, core.hooksPath points at the per-clone .git/hooks, and the only real hook present is untracked and machine-local. Consequences: a fresh clone or CI checkout has zero commit-time enforcement; a commit made from a terminal bypasses it; and every non-Claude agent this project explicitly supports and dispatches to — codex, opencode, antigravity, agy, claude-worker (src/shared/providers/providerFactory.ts) — bypasses it, with docs/reviews/antigravity-agent-commits-2026-07-21.md documenting Antigravity agents committing to this repo. Because the gate intercepts a shell command STRING rather than sitting in the commit path, it must reimplement machinery the standard seam provides free: a hand-rolled shell parser (.claude/hooks/shell-split.mjs, 159 lines) to find git commit among chained statements; a temp-index round-trip with its own journal, its own lock with a 10-minute staleness window and an interrupted-recovery path, because git stash --keep-index cannot faithfully restore a both-staged-and-modified file; and regex detection of --no-verify/core.hooksPath tokens anywhere in the command, which produces a defect the project accepted rather than fixed (durable-traps.md records that a commit whose MESSAGE names those tokens is rejected as if it were the bypass). That round-trip machinery has already produced a durable trap of its own — the gate round-trip clobber trap — so a commit gate that can lose work is one whose failure modes must be understandable in under a minute, and this one cannot be. All of these problems are artifacts of the wrong seam: lint-staged has solved staged-snapshot materialization including the stash edge cases, and lefthook or husky install real git hooks from tracked, versioned config so the gate binds for every client and every clone. The coupling has also hardened into the suite: tests/shared/shared-core-invariants.test.ts (INV-shared-core-16) asserts the hook exists AND that settings.json registers it as a PreToolUse hook, so the host dependency is now a tested contract. Recommendation: move the gate body into a tracked .githooks/pre-commit wired via core.hooksPath (set in postinstall) or lefthook, invoke the staged-snapshot check through lint-staged, split the remaining checks into one module per check behind a small declarative registry that check:guard-reach reconciles against (the shape scripts/guard-reach-data.mjs and src/audit/orchestrator/executors.ts already prove), and delete shell-split.mjs and the bypass-token regex entirely — a real pre-commit hook never parses a command line.

findings.title: The deliverable is an unbounded 1:1 dump of the machine contract — 17,941 lines and 1.29 MB whose navigable layer is the first 90 lines
findings.summary: Two perspectives found this independently and I re-verified the measurements: .audit-tools/audit-report.md is 1,288,977 bytes and 17,941 lines with roughly 1,495 heading sections, backed by a 1.9 MB audit-findings.json with 1480 findings, inside a 14 MB artifact tree. The README disclaims its fabricated counts; its structure is fabricated too (and its verdict vocabulary too — see DR-007). The handoff contract to the remediator is also not a decomposition: 5 work blocks cover all 1480 findings, averaging 296 findings per block, and src/audit/reporting/workBlocks.ts carries no target-size or budget notion, so the audit-to-remediate seam hands over buckets rather than units of work. Recommendation: define the human render as a digest with a hard budget and stop — executive summary, top risks, themes, work blocks, high-severity findings in full, and per-lens counts with a pointer into the JSON for the rest; optionally emit a separate full appendix for the rare reader who wants the enumeration, so the default artifact stays readable. Size work blocks to a bounded finding count in the same change. Everything below the fold already lives in the machine contract, which is the declared source of truth.

findings.title: The enforcement layer is the least-verified code in the repository, including the published entrypoint and the consumer postinstall
findings.summary: The project's answer to almost every risk is a mechanical guard — 22 check: gates, 13 hooks, a guard-reach registry, a doc manifest, attestations — and that strategy is correct. The question none of the other perspectives asked is who verifies the verifiers, and the answer is comparatively nothing. The typechecker covers src only (tsconfig.json includes ['src']); the test-tree config adds tests but sets checkJs:false (tsconfig.test.json). Nothing else is in any tsconfig, which leaves, all .mjs with zero .ts files: scripts/ (57 files, ~10,070 lines — every check: gate, release-and-publish.mjs, the nightly routine), .claude/hooks/ (12 files, ~3,010 lines — every pre-commit/trap/closeout gate), wrapper/ (12 files, ~4,126 lines), dispatch/, and both root bins: roughly 17,500 lines. vitest.config.ts additionally excludes .claude/**, so a test placed beside a hook never runs — which is why the hook contract tests had to be relocated under tests/. Two facts sharpen this beyond 'some scripts are untyped'. First, wrapper/ is not auxiliary — it is the shipped entrypoint (audit-code.mjs imports wrapper/audit-code-wrapper-lib.mjs, and wrapper/** is in package.json files), so the code every consumer executes first is outside the typechecker, as is scripts/postinstall.mjs, which runs on every consumer machine at install time (and per DR-038 mutates the consumer's repo). Second, the compensating control is itself hand-maintained data: check:guard-reach reconciles against scripts/guard-reach-data.mjs, a registry a human must remember to update — the hand-maintained-table pattern the project bans elsewhere, applied to the guards themselves. The risk is the shape, not today's correctness: the layer with the most authority (it blocks commits, rewrites docs, publishes releases, and runs on users' machines) has the weakest verification, and the ratio is rising — ~17.5k lines of guard machinery against ~129k lines of product, for a tool with two commands. The predictable failures are already an observed class here per the project's own records: a linked smoke drifted broken unnoticed, and ci stayed green across three commits while the only workflow running vitest was red. Recommendation: bring the enforcement layer under the regime it enforces rather than adding more guards on top of it — put scripts/, wrapper/, dispatch/, the root bins and .claude/hooks/ into a tsconfig with allowJs plus checkJs:true (JSDoc types where needed), and derive the guard-reach registry FROM the tree rather than declaring it against the tree. Also worth putting to the owner as a design question rather than a defect: whether the ratio of enforcement machinery to product still buys more than it costs, given that each new gate is itself unverified code that can fail open (see DR-004).

findings.title: The first thing a new user is asked is a provider cost-ordering table, before the tool has looked at the repo
findings.summary: Time-to-first-value is inverted: the tool demands a routing-economics decision before it has produced a single fact about the user's code. provider_confirmation is PRIORITY[0] in src/audit/orchestrator/nextStep.ts:26, ahead of repo_manifest and file_disposition, so intake cannot run until it is satisfied, and it always pauses on the interactive path — deliberately so even with one or zero auto-detected providers (src/audit/cli/nextStepHelpers.ts:2000-2003). What it presents (src/audit/cli/providerConfirmationStep.ts:323-483) is titled 'Confirm Provider Cost Ordering (Gate-0)', renders a blended dollars-per-Mtok table, and documents six optional response fields plus a six-row exclusion-axis grammar. A first-time user has at that moment no packets, no file count, no risk register, and no basis for reordering a cost table — the information that would make the question meaningful is produced by the intake step this gate blocks. A minimal run then takes at least seven next-step invocations plus a separate merge-and-ingest call per dispatch wave, across five always-interactive gates on default configuration (Gate-0, confirm-intent, design-review, dispatch, synthesis-narrative) and a sixth analyzer_install consent step on any repo missing an analyzer dependency, since auto is the default. There is no lightweight path: src/audit/orchestrator/trivialAudit.ts is a per-file coverage pruner rather than a mode, shallow depth is the only real dial, and force-synthesis is an operator recovery escape. Compounding this, the shipped loader tells the host that after the first next-step (the intake step) completes, confirm the audit scope (skills/audit-code/audit-code.prompt.md:90-91) — but the first next-step emits Gate-0, and scope_summary.json does not exist until the second. Recommendation, the single highest-leverage reordering available: move provider_confirmation to sit immediately after intake, so the user's first interaction is 'here is what I found in your repo, here is the proposed scope', and the routing question is asked once there is a packet count and a cost estimate to attach to it. That is a change to one array entry and its derivation, and it also fixes the loader's description.

findings.summary: candidates.ts builds the gitleaks argv as ['dir', root, ...] (src/audit/extractors/analyzers/candidates.ts:124-135) — the whole repo root, with no exclusion config and no reference to the audit's own scoping. But the intake executor produces repo_manifest + file_disposition BEFORE the acquisition executor runs (obligation order in src/audit/orchestrator/executors.ts:26 then :43), so a precise in-scope set already exists at spawn time: 1,397 manifested files, of which 1,210 are `included`, and node_modules/dist/.audit-tools-profile are all excluded (git check-ignore confirms all three are gitignored, and none appear in the manifest). Measured against this run's own external_analyzer_results.json: 310 gitleaks items resolving to just 11 distinct files, of which only 5 items (3 files) lie in the `included` set. 295 items — 95.2% of the entire output — come from ONE `excluded` file, .audit-tools-profile/vitest-history.ndjson, i.e. audit-tools' own profiling history. Another 10 come from paths not in the manifest at all: node_modules/@types/node, node_modules/zod and node_modules/knip/node_modules/zod test fixtures, dist/shared/quota/claudeOAuthQuotaSource.js (the compiled copy of a source file already scanned), and the tool's own .audit-tools/nightly/open-items.json + .audit-tools/audit/node-claims.json. So the default security tier walks a 147 MB node_modules tree plus 10.3 MB of dist to produce 98.4% noise, and it reports on the auditor's own state directory. Two consequences beyond the wasted walk: the noise is what forces a downstream reviewer to sift 310 items for 5 real ones, and every one of the 310 paths is persisted as an ABSOLUTE Windows path (C:\Code\audit-tools\...) while every other artifact keys files repo-relative with forward slashes, so the leads cannot be joined to their graph nodes without a normalization step. The fix is to pass the disposition-derived in-scope path set (or a generated exclusion config) through the buildArgv seam that today receives only `root`, and to relativize at the src/audit/adapters/normalizeExternal.ts adapter seam so acquired leads share the repo's path identity. NOTE this is NOT the .auditorignore-grammar issue: the audit's scoping worked correctly here and produced the right in-scope set — the acquired analyzer simply is never given it.

findings.title: The product will not report complete until the user files three categories of complaint about audit-tools
findings.summary: A development-process norm has been installed as a blocking gate in the end user's critical path. CLAUDE.md and docs/project-philosophy.md (B6) commit the project's own maintainers to log friction the moment they hit it across three named categories every lap; that commitment is now enforced against everyone who runs the tool. decideAuditFrictionCloseout (src/audit/orchestrator/nextStep.ts:181-186) folds a friction-triage gate into the terminal present_report step, and src/shared/friction/triage.ts:477-487 requires every entry of FRICTION_CATEGORIES to be covered by an observation or an explicit attestation, commenting that silence never counts. Until that holds, src/audit/cli/nextStepCommand.ts:598-624 emits status 'ready' rather than 'complete', with a stop condition telling the host to complete friction triage and call next-step again. The three required categories (src/shared/friction/frictionRecord.ts:44-48) are explicitly about audit-tools' own shortcomings: something the tool or prompt left to the host that it should have resolved, something the host had to remember or notice that the tool should guarantee, and a tool inefficiency. So a third party auditing their own repository must produce structured criticism of audit-tools, in three prescribed categories, before their run terminates cleanly. This inverts the value exchange at the exact moment the user has what they came for, and it makes the honest response (no friction) unrepresentable — which trains attestation-stamping and thereby corrupts the very signal the gate exists to collect. Recommendation: keep the instrumentation, which is genuinely valuable to the maintainer, but make it opt-in via a self-audit/dogfood flag, default off. If it stays on for third parties, an explicit 'no friction observed' must satisfy it, and the gate must never hold back terminal status.

findings.title: The remediation state store's unsafe primitive is the default path 25:4, and its documented safety precondition is a host-held guarantee the concurrency model makes false
findings.summary: RemediationState is the one artifact whose loss costs the user real work — it is what makes a remediation resumable. Two primitives write it and the unsafe one is the default. StateStore.mutate (src/remediate/state/store.ts:301-314) is the safe shape: read-modify-write entirely inside the lock (src/shared/io/lockedJsonStore.ts:104-117). StateStore.saveState (:322-327) delegates to replace, which takes the lock and writes the caller's whole object WITHOUT reading first (lockedJsonStore.ts:118-126), so the lock prevents a torn file but not a lost update: a caller that read at T0 and calls saveState at T1 silently discards everything a peer persisted in between. The docblock is admirably honest — no TOCTOU protection, no read, prefer mutate, use this only when the caller holds an external guarantee that no concurrent writer exists. The counts are the finding, and I re-verified them: saveState appears at 25 call sites in src/remediate, mutate at 4. The escape hatch became the highway. 'The caller holds an external guarantee' is precisely a host-discretion guarantee, the category A3 forbids, and nothing mechanically checks that a saveState caller holds the phase mutex, so a new call site ships green. Worse, the guarantee is contradicted by design intent: A9 wants arbitrary cooperative peers advancing one run, making 'no concurrent writer exists' false by construction. The phase:main mutex (src/remediate/steps/nextStep.ts:5475) is the only thing holding this together and does not cover everything that persists — countStep's closure ends in saveState (:5389-5395) and is invoked at :5463 before the mutex is acquired, writing a full state snapshot derived from a lockless read at :5345. The asymmetry is the design signal: the audit half solved this properly, claiming a bundle-mutation node, executing unlocked under a heartbeat, and re-validating ownership before persisting (src/audit/cli/auditStep.ts:243-258). This is one-core-two-draws breaking down in the most safety-critical substrate in the repo. Supporting detail: the signal that would let a de-claimed writer abandon its work exists and is dead — onRevoked (src/shared/quota/claimLease.ts:57-58,86-89) has zero production callers, only a test. Recommendation: delete saveState rather than document it, so the unsafe shape is unavailable; the recovery case it exists for (a corrupt on-disk state must not block recovery) is expressible as a mutate whose function ignores current, keeping the lock-held read-modify-write frame. Then wire onRevoked so a revoked claim abandons instead of finishing, and hoist the audit half's ownership re-validation into the shared core so both draws inherit it.

findings.title: The report's grounding summary hides the unverified 70%, making the README's central trust claim false on the tool's own output
findings.summary: README.md:85-86 states the product's core promise: every finding in the report is adversarially verified against current source by an independent reviewer before it is kept. The tool's own committed self-audit refutes it, and I re-verified every number directly from the artifact. .audit-tools/audit-findings.json holds 1480 findings, of which 1033 (70%) carry no grounding.status at all — 436 grounded, 11 ungrounded, 0 refuted. summary.grounding_status_breakdown persists exactly {grounded:436, ungrounded:11}, and the rendered summary prints those two numbers directly beneath 'Findings: 1480' in .audit-tools/audit-report.md — a breakdown summing to 447 presented without reconciliation against the population. A reader reasonably concludes 97.5% verification; the real figure is 29.5%. The mechanism is deliberate: groundingStatusBreakdown (src/audit/reporting/synthesis.ts:114-116) is countBy(findings, f => f.grounding?.status), and src/shared/countBy.ts skips undefined keys — its own docstring names this consumer, saying most findings have no grounding verdict at all. So the code knows the majority is unchecked and drops it from the tally. To be fair to the underlying work, the verification effort is well targeted: 74 of the 78 high-severity findings ARE grounded. The defect is purely in the reporting, which is what makes it worth fixing immediately — it costs the tool its credibility for no engineering gain. The repo already contains the exact pattern to copy: runtimeStatusBreakdown, eleven lines below in the same file (synthesis.ts:118-129), deliberately synthesizes a pending bucket for manifest entries with no result. Add an equivalent not_checked bucket so the counts sum to finding_count, and correct the README to state what is actually verified (high-severity findings) rather than every finding. See DR-007 for the separate and deeper question of what the grounded verdict itself proves.

findings.title: The shared obligation engine exports two non-composing selection APIs, and audit binds the general one degenerately — N identical executes that discard the engine's selection and re-decide
findings.summary: src/shared/engine/obligationEngine.ts contains two selection mechanisms rather than one: findFirstActionableObligation(priority, obligations), a scan over precomputed state values whose sole consumer is src/audit/orchestrator/nextStep.ts:97; and ObligationDef / findNextObligation / advance, the transition-and-emit loop used by the audit CLI fold, the audit orchestrator drain, and remediate. The module's own docstring says the second is a strict generalization of the bare scan, so the first is a special case that should not survive as a second public entry point — what the unification produced is a union of two vocabularies, not one mechanism. The degenerate binding is where it hurts. src/audit/orchestrator/advance.ts:441 builds one ObligationDef per PRIORITY id in which every def shares the identical execute (runDrainStep), and runDrainStep then throws the engine's selection away: it calls runSingleAdvanceStep, which re-runs decideNextStep from scratch to re-select. The comment at line 286 admits this — it always re-decides via decideNextStep and runs whatever that selects, regardless of which def's derive made it actionable. Three consequences, all present in the file. (1) Selection is computed twice per fold iteration by two different code paths, and their agreement rests on a prose claim (the identical id the engine's scan just picked, by construction, line 403) plus a doc-comment MUST in DecideNextStepOptions (nextStep.ts:110-121) warning that a gate-blind decideNextStep would disagree and dispatch the executor for a DIFFERENT obligation — a programmer-memory contract at the centre of the loop, in a project whose first principle is that correctness must never depend on someone remembering. (2) The ceremony had to be paid for: because findNextObligation calls every def's derive on the same bundle, the full computeStaleArtifacts content-hash pass would run once per PRIORITY entry per scan (~8-9x per the comment at line 336), so a per-call WeakMap memo was added purely to cancel the cost of the abstraction — a memo whose only job is to undo an abstraction's overhead is the receipt for a bad fit. (3) deriveObligationState is duplicated between advance.ts:350 and nextStepHelpers.ts:1902, with a comment electing to keep a trivial copy rather than share across the cli/orchestrator boundary. That the elegant form is reachable is proven in the same repo: src/shared/dispatch/unifiedRolling.ts embeds audit as the read-only degenerate case, passing a single level of read-only nodes that ownershipSubWaves collapses into one maximal parallel sub-wave so the level machinery no-ops — no second selection, no memo, no by-construction comment. Recommendation: make the selected obligation BE the dispatch (look its executor up on the selected id), delete the second decideNextStep call inside the fold, delete the memo, and retire findFirstActionableObligation from the public surface.

findings.title: The tool instructs its reviewing agents to ingest the audited repository's own agent-instruction files, making indirect prompt injection a mandated behavior rather than a host mistake
findings.summary: Where DR-001 is the audited repo causing EXECUTION, this is the audited repo causing INFLUENCE — and it is worse in one respect: the tool does not merely fail to defend against it, it explicitly directs it. conceptualCritiqueInstructions() emits, verbatim, an instruction to read the project's own documentation first — its README, anything under docs/, design notes, and any CLAUDE.md/agent-instruction files — to learn what the project is trying to be (src/audit/orchestrator/designReviewPrompt.ts:312, abbreviated again at :676). Every conceptual-review prompt therefore instructs an agent that, in the conversation-first design, holds Read/Edit/Bash and the operator's credentials, to read the audited repository's agent-instruction files and treat them as intent-establishing guidance. There is no untrusted framing, no instruction to disregard directives found there, and no test. Because it is tool-authored, it is squarely an A3 violation: safety depends on the host independently deciding to distrust text the tool told it to trust. The same channel exists more diffusely wherever repo-derived strings are interpolated into instruction bodies rather than fenced as data: verbatim source lines become instruction bullets (fileAnchors.ts:305-330 puts a raw line of the audited file into detail, rendered as a markdown bullet by packetPrompt.ts:39-40, triggered by a KEYWORD_PATTERN that matches any line containing TODO); file bodies are inlined between forgeable delimiters (openAiCompatibleProvider.ts:739-741 wraps the body in BEGIN/END CURRENT FILE markers with no scan of the body for the terminator, so a file containing that line closes its own block early); and the design-review prompt interpolates flow names, risk signals, route strings lifted from source, finding titles and charter purposes uniformly into its markdown instruction body (designReviewPrompt.ts:59,77,136,171,417). A second-order channel: a prior pass's LLM-authored summary is carried in task.rationale and re-rendered as instruction text (packetPrompt.ts:255,263), so one compromised pass steers the next. Why this matters more here than in a typical agent product: audit-code's output is a trust artifact a human acts on, and remediate-code consumes that artifact to WRITE CODE. An injected instruction need not exfiltrate anything — suppressing findings in one file, or adding a plausible finding whose remediation introduces a flaw, is sufficient, and the pipeline carries it end to end. Partial mitigations worth crediting: truncate collapses whitespace (fileAnchors.ts:134-139) so injected text cannot forge a new markdown line, and commentDecomposition.ts already demonstrates the safe pattern by reducing repo comments to CouplingEdge{a,b,weight} via includes() checks so the text never reaches a prompt. Recommendation: route every interpolation of target-repo content through a single asUntrustedData() helper that fences it in a non-forgeable envelope (per-run random delimiter, or JSON-encoding so no raw line can terminate the block) and prefixes a standing frame naming it as possibly-hostile data that must never be followed as instruction; change the :312 directive to say exactly that about the repo's README/docs/CLAUDE.md instead of presenting them as authoritative intent. The interpolation sites are few and already centralized in three renderers, and the property is pinnable by a contract test asserting no renderer concatenates repo content outside the helper — which is how the rest of this codebase makes properties true.

findings.title: The tree-sitter parse tier cannot work in any published install, and the report never says the graph was degraded
findings.summary: Two perspectives found the two halves of this — the packaging defect and the missing fidelity disclosure — and they are one finding because either alone understates it. Tree-sitter is the correct modern choice for language-neutral parsing and the project uses the right variant (web-tree-sitter WASM, pure JS, no native build), but the packaging makes it unreachable for users. web-tree-sitter and tree-sitter-wasms are declared in devDependencies (verified: no optionalDependencies block exists in package.json), so npm install -g audit-tools does not install them. src/audit/extractors/analyzers/treeSitter.ts:137-152 resolves grammar files exclusively through requireFromHere.resolve('tree-sitter-wasms/out/tree-sitter-<lang>.wasm') — i.e. from audit-tools' own install tree — with no audited-repo path and no version-keyed cache path, so resolveAnalyzerDep cannot help. The build does not ship them either: scripts/shared/copy-data-assets.mjs copies only src/shared/data/**/*.json, and dist/ contains no .wasm. Self-install is impossible too: src/audit/extractors/analyzers/python.ts declares dependency 'web-tree-sitter' with no version, and installToCache hard-rejects an unversioned spec. Net effect: in the shipped product the Python, HTML and CSS graph analyzers ALWAYS degrade to the regex floor in src/audit/extractors/graph.ts, the higher-confidence edges (0.96-0.97) designed to win over the 0.95 floor never materialize outside this repo's own checkout, and the enrichment layer that makes non-JS ecosystems first-class is the layer that never runs — which directly undercuts the language-neutrality claim. Code and comments call the tier an optional dependency (registry.ts:16-18, analyzers/types.ts:10-11) but as declared it is dev-only, so the intended graceful-optional story and the shipped reality differ. The second half is that the degradation is invisible where it matters most. Breadth of coverage IS reported well — budget-deferred tasks and pool-exhausted units appear in both the contract and the markdown (synthesis.ts:393-398) plus a Scope and Coverage section (:510-521) — but fidelity is not: analyzers_used is persisted on the graph bundle (graphEnrichmentExecutor.ts:164-168) and knipGraphCrosscheck.ts:137-139 correctly marks a lead UNVERIFIED when the relevant analyzer did not run, yet nothing under src/audit/reporting/ reads analyzers_used or the tooling manifest, and getTreeSitterDegradationCount (treeSitter.ts:58-60) is write-only in production with tests as its only readers. So a user auditing a Python repo gets the regex floor and the report says nothing. Recommendation: promote web-tree-sitter and tree-sitter-wasms to dependencies (or declare them in optionalDependencies as a deliberate choice), add the grammar directory to the build asset copy and to package.json files so the WASM ships in the tarball, give resolveGrammarPath the repo-then-cache-then-bundled chain the TypeScript analyzer already has, pin a version on the tree-sitter analyzer declarations so cache install can succeed, and emit the analyzer plan's per-analyzer resolution plus the degradation count into the findings contract with a Scope-and-Coverage line whenever any in-scope language fell back — the same honest-degradation treatment ungrounded findings already receive. Note the interaction with DR-001(a): today the only way the tier is present is when the AUDITED repo happens to ship it, which is the hazard rather than a feature.

findings.title: The write-scope gate does not confine a worker to its declared write scope — it only arbitrates cross-block collisions, so a single-block wave has no confinement at all
findings.summary:
INFERRED CONTRACT: the names and the surrounding docs all assert confinement — `enforceWriteScope`, `writeScopeViolations`, "Worker edited files outside its declared write scope" (src/remediate/steps/dispatch/writeScope.ts:58), and CLAUDE.md lists "write-scope enforcement" among the properties that must be guaranteed by the tool rather than by the host remembering. A reader reasonably infers: a worker's edits are restricted to its declared `write_paths`.

COUNTEREXAMPLE: the effective rule is `blocked ⟺ ∃ edited file f ∉ declaredScope(thisBlock) ∧ f ∈ declaredScope(someSiblingBlock)`. Any out-of-declared edit to a file NO SIBLING declared is granted and widens the node's effective scope (`adjudicateWriteScope`, writeScope.ts:106-147, and its own docstring at :97-99). Verified by running the shipped code with an edit set of `{src/declared.ts, src/UNDECLARED.ts, package.json, .github/workflows/release.yml}` against a block declaring only `src/declared.ts`:
  single block                          → `{blocked: false}`
  two blocks, sibling declares src/other.ts → `{blocked: false}`
  sibling declares package.json             → `{blocked: true}` (seam conflict)
  empty registry                            → `{blocked: false}`
So on a single-block wave the gate cannot block on scope at all: a worker may rewrite `package.json`, a release workflow, or any other file in the tree and the accept passes. The same holds when the dispatch plan cannot be read and `allBlockScopes` degrades to `[]` (documented as "a sound no-op, never a skip" at acceptNode.ts:86-87).

ASSESSMENT: the grant behaviour is deliberate and test-pinned (tests/remediate/dispatch-evidence-and-writescope.test.ts:587-591, "GRANTS an edit to an UNOWNED file no sibling declared") — the finding is not that the code disagrees with its own tests, but that the CONTRACT the rest of the system advertises is confinement while the mechanism provides only collision arbitration. Two real consequences: (a) `write_paths` is not a safety boundary, so nothing mechanically prevents a remediation worker from editing infrastructure it was never scoped to; (b) the declared scope is load-bearing elsewhere (verification commands, region ownership scheduling) yet is silently mutable by the worker's actual behaviour.

RECOMMENDED CHANGE: separate the two questions rather than conflating them in one predicate. Keep seam arbitration as-is, but add a genuine confinement boundary that does not depend on sibling declarations — e.g. a per-run "never writable" set (lockfiles, CI workflows, `package.json`, release scripts) that blocks regardless of ownership, and require an explicit widening record (not a silent grant) when a node edits outside its declared scope. If unowned-grant must stay the default, rename the mechanism to what it does (`adjudicateCrossBlockOwnership`) so no future reader infers a confinement guarantee that was never there.
