findings.title: Twelve-plus validation runs, zero clean completions, and routine operator rescue — the North Star is contradicted by the operating record while capability keeps being added
findings.summary: The stated North Star (docs/project-philosophy.md) is that the tool must be trustworthy even when the host agent is weak, and that no correctness property may depend on the host being careful or clever. The backlog is a detailed record of the opposite, and it is being treated as a queue of defects rather than as evidence about the approach. Across docs/backlog/open-bugs.md and docs/backlog/forward-tracks.md there are at least twelve distinct dogfood attempts between 2026-07-04 and 2026-07-24, none recorded as a clean completion: a 313-packet run invalidated back to charter_extraction (open-bugs.md:511); a lane benched mid-run BY HAND, host discretion (:115); an operator top_k change with zero effect until a module was hand-imported from dist with force:true (:360-361); the host having to manually relay every completion to the dispatcher (:911-915); a next-step exceeding a 2-minute command timeout with no heartbeat, forcing a blind retry to see whether it was wedged or working (:680); a drain that re-stormed a cooling lane to 143 consecutive 429s (:357-358); 44 of 55 agents killed by a session limit (:479-481); a completion livelock from claims released only at merge (:77). Recovery routinely requires force-synthesis plus git branch --no-merged main to hand-merge stranded commits (durable-traps.md:384-393, open-bugs.md:888-894). Meanwhile roughly 21 entries carry an explicit live-run watch marker and about 32 are live-gated in total, all waiting on evidence from a run that has never cleanly happened, against 109 open work entries. The structural risk is not any individual defect: it is that capability keeps being added while the validation channel stays closed, so each new mechanism is unvalidated and the set of things one clean run must simultaneously survive keeps growing — which is why nearly every other finding in this review is about a mechanism whose behavior under load nobody has observed. Recommendation: freeze feature work and buy a single green run on a small pinned external repository, not on audit-tools itself (DR-002 shows why self-audit and self-development are mutually exclusive). The A2 oracle corpus described in forward-tracks.md:108-126 is the right instrument and is already scoped as small, public, pinned repos; promote it from funded-but-not-the-current-track to the current track, because every live-run watch entry is blocked behind it.

findings.title: Write-scope and merge-state gates are inert on the host-driven main-tree dispatch paths, leaving prompt text and worker self-report as the only control
findings.summary:
INFERRED CONTRACT: the project's central invariant — "Auditor-agnostic robustness — enforce in tooling, never host discretion... Any place the workflow only works because a capable host folded in guidance... is a latent failure mode" (CLAUDE.md). For remediation the two tool-owned guarantees are the write-scope gate and the merge-state gate that distinguishes edits that actually LANDED from a worker that merely self-reported `resolved` ("OBL-DS-06: never trust the worker's self report", src/remediate/steps/dispatch/acceptNode.ts:777-781).

COUNTEREXAMPLE: both gates are structurally unreachable on the dispatch paths that run nodes in the operator's real checkout instead of a per-node worktree. The enforcement chain is `executeNodeInWorktree` → `acceptNodeWorktree` → `enforceAcceptWriteScope` (acceptNode.ts:565-576), and the ground truth it consumes is a per-node branch diff (`git diff --name-only HEAD...<branch>`, common.ts:166-170). With no worktree there is no branch, so there is no diff and no gate. The codebase states this outright in two places: "The write-scope gate itself is NOT applied here: it runs at ACCEPT time... A missing branch means the interim main-tree path was used (no per-worker diff): nothing to collect" (marshal.ts:1294-1300), and "the interim main-tree path writes none, so the merge-state gate is inert there" (acceptNode.ts:782). The affected paths include the non-rolling host fan-out `dispatch_implement` and `implement_rolling_sequential` (src/remediate/steps/nextStep.ts, the `dispatch_implement` and sequential branches), where the surviving controls are prompt text (implementPrompt.ts) and the worker's self-reported `amended_files` (marshal.ts:891-900) — i.e. precisely the "host remembering" and "worker self-report" that the invariant forbids.

WHY THIS IS A COVERAGE GAP RATHER THAN A BUG: each gate is correct where it runs; what is missing is that the guarantee is advertised as a property of remediation while being a property of *one dispatch topology*. Nothing marks the main-tree paths as unsafe to an operator, and nothing prevents a future path from inheriting the same hole. The repo's own memory note "a script in no gate is not a gate" is the same failure shape one level up.

RECOMMENDED CHANGE: make the enforcement unconditional on topology. Either (a) require worktree isolation for every implement dispatch and delete the main-tree paths (consistent with the project's stated preference for deleting legacy paths over keeping a lighter half-measure), or (b) give the main-tree path an equivalent tool-owned ground truth — snapshot `git status --porcelain`/a tree hash before dispatch and diff after, then run the SAME `adjudicateWriteScope` and merge-state logic against that edit set. Whichever is chosen, add a contract test asserting that every dispatch path reaching a provider also reaches a write-scope adjudication, so a third path cannot be added gate-free.

findings.title: Acyclicity of the DAG-is-truth artifact graph is preserved by prose arguments and by omitting a real edge, and LLM-authored nodes sit under byte-exact staleness
findings.summary: The load-bearing axiom is that artifacts are continuity and the dependency DAG is truth — staleness propagates along one explicit acyclic relation, never ad-hoc checks. src/audit/orchestrator/dependencyMap.ts implements it well in one respect worth crediting: ARTIFACT_DEPENDS_ON_MAP is the single hand-authored adjacency and the forward view is computed by invertDependencyMap, so there is exactly one hand-authored adjacency representation and everything else is computed from it. But the relation the domain actually has is not acyclic, and the map keeps it acyclic by argument rather than by construction. Across 25 nodes there are five separate acyclicity arguments in comments (lines 48, 108, 141, 164, 167), three of the same form: no cycle, because the executor writes X AND Y in one advanceAudit call, dependency-first. That is not the absence of a cycle — it is a cycle whose two endpoints are written atomically, so the ordering inside the pair never has to be resolved. And one comment concedes the graph is missing a real edge to stay acyclic: access-memory is a genuine input to packet composition, but the dependency threads in at the dispatch code level rather than as a DAG edge, to avoid a coverage-to-results-to-access_memory-to-coverage cycle (line 167). So the artifact declared to be truth is knowingly incomplete, and the omitted edge is exactly the kind of feedback the audit pipeline is built on. A second, related strain: several interior nodes are LLM-authored (charter_register.json is produced by the LLM charter pass and is upstream of both charter_clarification.json and systemic_challenge.json) while the staleness algebra is exact content-hash equality, so any source edit re-stales the register, whose regenerated bytes will differ even when its meaning does not, cascading two further expensive LLM passes. The repo already knows this hazard for deterministic extractors — the stable-array-order rule exists precisely because incidental ordering silently churns a content hash and cascades phantom staleness — but for a non-deterministic producer that mitigation is unavailable, so the assumption that hash inequality implies downstream invalidity is unsound on exactly the nodes where re-running is most expensive. Recommendation, the standard clean-sheet formulation for both strains: make the atomic write-set a first-class node. Executors already declare their write-sets as data — tests/audit/seam-dependency-map-executor-writeset-parity.test.ts recovers them by reading executor module source text to cross-check the map — so the ingredients exist. Group artifacts by the write-set that produces them, define dependencies between groups, and acyclicity becomes a property the tool checks on the condensation (an SCC condensation is always a DAG) instead of five prose arguments and one deliberately-missing edge; that also gives the omitted access-memory dependency a legal home. Separately, mark LLM-authored nodes with a semantic rather than byte freshness key so a regenerated-but-equivalent artifact does not fan out three LLM re-runs.

findings.title: The state and coordination layer hand-rolls a transactional multi-writer store on the filesystem; an embedded SQL engine would delete ~4,000 lines and an entire class of liveness bugs
findings.summary: The project persists run state as JSON files guarded by a hand-built advisory-lock stack: src/shared/quota/fileLock.ts (293 lines), src/shared/io/lockedJsonStore.ts, claimRegistry.ts, claimLease.ts, reservationLedger.ts, quota/state.ts, src/remediate/state/store.ts, src/remediate/contractPipeline/artifactStore.ts, plus temp-then-rename atomic writes in src/shared/io/json.ts and staleness bookkeeping in staleness.ts / artifactMetadata.ts — 3,946 lines across those files alone. Nearly all of the hardest logic exists for ONE reason: a filesystem lock cannot detect a dead holder. That single gap is why the code needs STALE_LOCK_MS (30s), owner tokens, mtime heartbeats, a .steal sidecar claim to serialize stale removal, token-checked reclaim, and Windows EPERM/EACCES retry paths. The file's own comments record that the first implementation admitted a real double-hold race (two stealers both believing they held the lock), fixed by adding the sidecar — precisely the class of bug a mature library has already absorbed. The 30s window then leaks upward as a standing design tension: src/audit/cli/auditStep.ts:121, src/remediate/steps/nextStep.ts:2632, src/shared/dispatch/admissionLoop.ts:374 and src/remediate/state/store.ts:231 all reason explicitly about heartbeating inside or timing out under STALE_LOCK_MS. An embedded SQL engine makes the apparatus unnecessary: a BEGIN IMMEDIATE transaction is kernel-mediated per connection, so a crashed peer's lock releases IMMEDIATELY rather than after a 30-second heuristic — no stale window, no heartbeat, no steal race, no token protocol; a UNIQUE constraint on node_id expresses claim exclusivity directly; and WAL mode gives concurrent readers with a single writer for free. This matters most for the direction actively being built: spec/multi-ide-concurrent-runs-design.md targets an arbitrary number of agents cooperating on ONE shared run with ClaimRegistry plus withFileLock as its stated substrate — i.e. a genuine multi-process transactional workload implemented on advisory file locks — and the three gaps that spec enumerates (a coarse lock serializing peers, no task-level claiming, a single clobbered step slot) are all standard SQL problems. Recommendation: adopt node:sqlite (built into Node, zero dependencies, no native build — strictly better than the project's own pure-JS-so-OS-agnostic bar) for run state, claims and the artifact/staleness ledger, keeping the JSON/markdown deliverables as rendered exports; the cost is raising the engines.node floor above 20. Confidence is medium and one genuine disagreement is worth recording rather than resolving: the adversarial perspective independently judged fileLock.ts unusually careful and correct (exclusive wx create with owner token, bounded backoff clamped to time-remaining, a live-holder heartbeat at one third of the stale window, stale-steal serialized through its own sidecar with a token re-check before unlink, and timeout as a THROW rather than proceeding unlocked). Both readings are compatible — this is a careful implementation of a mechanism that may not need to exist — but a migration trades a well-understood, well-tested substrate for a new one, and DR-010 is a lost-update defect that should be fixed on the current substrate regardless of this decision. Note the project already tolerates SQLite in its environment: src/shared/quota/antigravityQuotaSource.ts shells out to the sqlite3 CLI to read a host token.

findings.title: .auditorignore promises gitignore-shaped scoping but implements none of the semantics — globs and negations are silent no-ops
findings.summary: src/audit/extractors/ignore.ts is 21 lines, and its entire parser splits on newlines, trims, and drops blank lines and comments. The matcher, in src/audit/extractors/fsIntake.ts:33-44, is plain path-segment comparison: equals, startsWith(value + '/'), includes('/' + value + '/'), endsWith('/' + value). Nothing handles glob patterns, negation, leading-slash anchoring, trailing-slash directory-only semantics, or character classes. So an operator writing a wildcard, a recursive directory pattern, or a negation into .auditorignore gets a silently inert line — the audit scope is wrong and nothing reports it. The file name deliberately evokes .gitignore, and src/audit/orchestrator/intakeExecutors.ts:613 tells the user their files may have been filtered by .auditorignore, so the format's semantics are implied to the operator without being implemented. This is the exact failure mode the project's own two-tier dependency policy names — a hand-rolled scanner silently dropping what it does not understand — and the fix is the one the policy prescribes: the ignore npm package is pure JS, has no native build, is the de-facto implementation of gitignore semantics (used by ESLint and Prettier), and would replace both files with a few lines. The inconsistency is sharper because the project gets the harder case RIGHT: src/audit/extractors/disposition.ts:181-249 deliberately does not reimplement gitignore, batching a single git check-ignore --stdin -z instead, with exit-code contract handling and a sanity guard. Recommendation: back .auditorignore with the ignore package (or delegate to git check-ignore with an extra exclude file, matching the existing disposition path), and until then reject or warn on any line containing glob or negation syntax rather than accepting it as a literal segment.

findings.title: `external_acquisition` has no branch in the session-config validator, so a non-string `consent_token` reaches the spawn gate and throws an uncaught TypeError
findings.summary:
INFERRED CONTRACT: `session-config.json` is operator-authored, hand-edited (there is no CLI flag for these fields), and therefore untrusted input that must be validated before use. The project states the rule as a durable principle — project memory records "Validate BEFORE migrate" and "a validator guards every field the caller reads" — and `validateSessionConfig` (src/shared/validation/sessionConfig.ts, ~1030 lines) implements exactly that for the rest of the config.

COUNTEREXAMPLE: `external_acquisition` is a known key (so `warnUnknownKeys` stays silent) but has NO type-checking branch — grepped `src/shared/validation/sessionConfig.ts` for `external_acquisition`: zero occurrences. Its declared shape is `{ enabled?: boolean; consent_token?: string }` (src/shared/types/sessionConfig.ts:696-699), but nothing enforces that at load. The value flows unchecked from `loadSessionConfig` through `nextStepCommand.ts:580` into `admitSpawn`, which calls `.trim()` on it (acquisitionEngine.ts:223). Verified by running the shipped code: `consent_token` of `1`, `true`, `{}`, and `["x"]` each throw `TypeError: consentToken.trim is not a function`. The call site at acquisitionEngine.ts:305 is not wrapped in try/catch (confirmed by reading acquisitionEngine.ts:298-318), so the throw escapes the analyzer-acquisition step rather than degrading to a `skipped` status the way every other failure in that function does.

WHY IT MATTERS: the failure is fail-closed with respect to spawning (nothing runs) but fail-loud-and-unhandled with respect to the run — a single mistyped JSON value in a hand-edited config aborts the step instead of producing the actionable validation error the rest of the config would produce. It is also the exact defect CLASS the project's own memory principle names, so the fix belongs at the validator, not at the call site.

RECOMMENDED CHANGE: add an `external_acquisition` branch to `validateSessionConfig` that checks it is a record, that `enabled` is boolean when present, and that `consent_token` is a string when present — so a bad value surfaces as a validation issue at load with the file and field named. Since the field is read by a security gate, prefer rejecting the config over coercing. A defensive `typeof consentToken === "string"` guard in `admitSpawn` is worth adding too, but as a second layer, not as the fix.

findings.title: 87% of verify:checks is a single leg, because the expensive audit flow is executed twice per release for two installation shapes that differ only in bootstrap
findings.summary: The repo's own always-on profiling record (.audit-tools-profile/verify-checks-latest.json) measures verify:checks at 241,080 ms, of which smoke:packaged-audit-code alone is 210,611 ms - 87.4%. Every other leg combined is 30.5 s, and the fourteen doc/tree check legs total ~7.0 s, so parallelizing the cheap legs would recover almost nothing; the entire cost is one leg. That leg's runtime is the shared flow: smoke-packaged-audit-code.mjs and smoke-linked-audit-code.mjs both import runEnsurePhase / runInstallPhase / runAuditFlowPhase / withTempRepo from the same 719-line scripts/audit/smoke-audit-flow.mjs and invoke them with identical arguments, and verify:release runs verify:checks (containing the packaged smoke) AND then smoke:linked-audit-code - so the full ensure + install + next-step/ingest-results/present_report flow is driven end-to-end twice per release. The two smokes' genuinely distinct assertions are only the installation-shape ones each uniquely owns (tarball file-list contract, .bin shim resolution, isolated npm env, prompt-path resolution, postinstall side effects). Run the expensive flow ONCE against whichever install shape is authoritative and reduce the sibling to its bootstrap-surface contract - the shape the remediate pair already has - and verify:checks drops from ~4 min to well under 1 min with no loss of distinct coverage. Because this leg also gates every commit path that runs the checks, it is the single largest lever on developer-loop latency in the repo.

findings.title: A 129,000-line TypeScript repo that audits other people's maintainability has no linter and no formatter; roughly 7,200 lines of bespoke .mjs gates stand in their place
findings.summary: package.json declares no ESLint, Biome, oxlint, Prettier or dprint — the only static discipline over 522 source files and 129,284 lines is tsc --strict. In place of a linter the project maintains a bespoke governance layer: ~3,010 lines of .claude/hooks/*.mjs, ~2,203 lines of scripts/check-*.mjs, ~1,483 lines of generate/verify gate helpers, ~520 lines of registry data modules, and 106 test files that read the source tree and assert properties over it. A substantial fraction reimplements rules an off-the-shelf linter provides declaratively: scripts/check-control-bytes.mjs enforces no byte below 0x20 except tab/LF/CR after being bitten twice, where no-control-regex and no-irregular-whitespace are stock rules; the layering and loop-core boundary rules currently expressed as bespoke INV-* tests plus a generated pattern list (.claude/hooks/loop-core-patterns.mjs, src/shared/loopCorePaths.ts) are exactly no-restricted-imports / import-x no-restricted-paths territory; TODO-comment bans, import cycles, unused locals and consistent type-only imports are all stock. The cost is not only volume: each bespoke gate is its own regex over source text, so each carries its own false-positive surface — the commit-message false positive in DR-009 is one instance — and none of them compose or report through a common diagnostic channel. The project's own principle that guards should be declared DATA rather than prose (realized well in scripts/guard-reach-data.mjs) argues FOR a rule-config-driven linter, not against it. Recommendation: adopt a flat-config linter (oxlint or Biome if gate wall-clock matters, typescript-eslint if type-aware rules are wanted), port the mechanically expressible gates to rules, and delete the corresponding .mjs scripts and tree-scanning tests in the same atomic change the project's own conventions require. Keep bespoke gates only for the genuinely project-specific properties no rule engine can express — doc-manifest coverage, philosophy-brief generation, guard-reach reconciliation.

findings.title: A configured api_key_env that resolves empty silently degrades to the dummy sentinel key instead of refusing the launch

findings.title: A private identifier language is load-bearing in code, and the glossary documents that its ids are not unique
findings.summary: The tree runs roughly 20 opaque id families (INV-, CE-, N-, SEAM-, FND-, plus 11 lens prefixes) as load-bearing handles in comments, obligation ids and filenames. docs/glossary-ids.md exists precisely because of this and opens by admitting that these ids are load-bearing in comments and obligation ids but defined nowhere a reader can look them up. The glossary then documents that the scheme fails at the one property an identifier exists to provide: CE-* is flagged not globally unique, and the CE-002 row states that the bare id is reused as a local counterexample-class marker at several unrelated sites rather than one shared concept, listing five files, with the instruction to always resolve a CE-* id from its own document and never assume cross-document uniqueness. Elsewhere INV-S05 and INV-QD-11 are the same invariant under two ids, INV-o3 is lowercase where every sibling is uppercase, INV-DC1-6 and INV-DC2-3 encode ranges inside a single id, and the INV-QD row spends a paragraph tracking which files carry the literal token and which merely implement the behavior. The guard (tests/shared/id-glossary.test.ts) is honest about its own reach — scoped to families, not individual ids — so it covers the case a reader never hits (a new family) and cannot cover the case a reader always hits (an individual id in a comment): enforcement is aimed at the wrong unit. The cost lands hardest in filenames: 28 test files are named for these ids (tests/audit/dc1.test.ts, dc2.test.ts, a2.test.ts, f1.test.ts, inv2.test.ts, tests/remediate/dc3.test.ts through dc6.test.ts). A failing test named dc4.test.ts tells you nothing about what broke; you must resolve a historical redesign-node number before you can start. The glossary's own closing note concedes these are spent: nodes are consumed once, their work folds into the durable code, and the ids survive only as cross-refs in comments. Recommendation: apply the fix the glossary already prescribes at its own lines 13-14 — inline the one-sentence statement at the primary definition site so the id becomes an optional cross-ref rather than the only handle — rename the 28 id-named test files after what they assert, and delete the historical N-* and single-letter families whose work has already folded in. Live invariants keep their ids as cross-references next to a readable statement, not as the only handle.

findings.title: Anchor argument policy does not confine inspection to the audited repo: `git --git-dir=`, `--work-tree=`, and absolute search positionals are admitted
findings.summary:
INFERRED CONTRACT: the anchor pass inspects the repository under audit. The runner is handed `cwd = repoRoot` (src/audit/validation/anchorGrounding.ts:178), the argument policy is default-deny and curated per executable specifically so "positionals (search patterns / file paths) are allowed — they name what to inspect, not code to run" (src/shared/tooling/allowlistedExec.ts:18-20), and `git` gets extra treatment because its options can escape read-only inspection (`GIT_REFUSED_OPTIONS`, :195-203).

COUNTEREXAMPLE: nothing confines *which files* are inspected. The permitted positional is any string, including an absolute path outside the repo, and git's cwd-redirecting options are not in the refused set. Verified by running the shipped code:
  `["git","--git-dir=C:/other/.git","log"]`   → allowed: true
  `["git","--work-tree=C:/other","status"]`   → allowed: true
  `["grep","-r","secret","C:/Users"]`         → allowed: true
  `["rg","--hidden","AKIA","C:/Users/ethan"]`  → allowed: true
(`["git","-C","dir","log"]` is refused, but only incidentally — the separated `dir` positional is mistaken for the subcommand and fails the read-only-subcommand check, so the protection is an accident of the parser rather than a rule. The `--git-dir=`/`--work-tree=` attached forms sail through.)

WHY IT MATTERS: combined with model-authored `confirm_if` (DR-001), each anchor is a one-bit read oracle over an arbitrary filesystem path: `rg --hidden 'AKIA[A-Z0-9]{16}' C:/Users/<user>` with `confirm_if: {kind: "output_includes", text: "AKIA"}` returns confirmed exactly when such a string exists, and the persisted evidence line records the command that was run (`anchorEvidenceLine`, anchorGrounding.ts:240). The `--hidden`/`--no-ignore` flags are on the allowlist, so dotfile directories are in reach. This is not bulk exfiltration — only the summary line, not the captured output, is folded into `finding.evidence` (mergeAndIngestCommand.ts:619-623) — but it is an unbounded read predicate over the host filesystem authored by the model, which is a strictly larger boundary than "inspect the audited repo".

RECOMMENDED CHANGE: containment-check every positional the same way DR-003 recommends for cited paths — reject any argument that `resolveWithinRoot(repoRoot, arg)` does not place inside the audited root (with an allowance for pattern arguments, which are distinguishable by position for each allowlisted tool). Add `--git-dir`, `--work-tree`, and `--namespace` (attached and separated forms) to `GIT_REFUSED_OPTIONS`, and make the read-only-subcommand check positional-aware rather than "first token not starting with `-`".

findings.title: Charter delta (spec drift) in subsystem scripts/nightly/answer.mjs
findings.summary: 'Permanent against the SUBJECT — not the report, file SHA, or wording' holds only against the REPORT file. subjectKey() in items.mjs hashes `<path>::<normalizeSubject(prose)>`, and normalization is whitespace + lowercase only — so the key still carries both the source doc's path and the prose wording. Relocating an unchanged claim (exactly what the routine's own docs leg does when it condenses or splits a doc, e.g. the backlog.md → docs/backlog/*.md split) mints a new key and legitimately re-asks a settled question. Already materialized: 14 of 88 entries in .claude/nightly-decisions.json name paths absent from the tree (spec/audit/dispatch-admission-control.md x4, spec/host-validation.md, spec/dispatch-jit-claims.md, docs/quota-dispatch-design.md, docs/model-capability-ranking-sources.md, examples/9router-harness-proxy-setup.md). The reword half is explicitly deliberated in-module ('a reword is a new item'); the PATH half is deliberated nowhere and is the file-keyed residue the charter claims to have removed.

findings.title: cli.ts dispatcher guard tests are hand-copied tables that have already drifted in both copies
findings.summary: Two test files hand-maintain copies of cli.ts's command surface, and both have decayed. tests/audit/cli-dispatcher.test.ts's KNOWN_COMMANDS mirrors the switch in src/audit/cli.ts but omits 'force-synthesis', 'score-audit' and 'score-tokens' (all present in cli.ts's switch and its Available-commands message); because the assertion is inclusion-only, the missing entries pass silently — the drift guard no longer guards new commands. The duplication is the defect: the command registry should be exported once from cli.ts (or derived from the switch) and both tests should consume that single source, making the two decayed copies unnecessary.

findings.title: Closing-action authority is flat across a steep blast-radius gradient: one pre_authorized bit waives the preview for publish exactly as for commit
findings.summary: The remediate half ends by taking a real action on the user's world. The four actions — commit, push, open-pr, publish (src/remediate/state/closingActions.ts:2-5) — span an enormous range of reversibility: a local commit is trivially undone; publishing to a package registry is public, immediate, and effectively immutable. The authority model does not reflect that range. All four are in PREVIEW_ACTIONS and get a confirmation preview by default, which is right (src/remediate/phases/close.ts:717), but checkClosingPreview short-circuits on a single boolean BEFORE it looks at which action is involved — pre_authorized === true returns immediately (close.ts:730) and only then does it consult PREVIEW_ACTIONS. One bit therefore waives the preview for publish on exactly the same terms as for commit. The deeper mismatch is temporal rather than merely granular: per the product's own flow the operator sets the closing action and pre-authorization UP FRONT, before planning and implementation run, so consent is granted before the artifact it authorizes exists. At confirmation time the operator does not know the file list, the diff, the version that will be published, or whether the review gate auto-approved anything. For a local commit that is a reasonable trade for autonomy; for an irreversible public release it means the one human checkpoint occurs at the point of minimum information. Note also that custom_command proceeds without preview by construction (close.ts:731 — it is not in PREVIEW_ACTIONS) and is argv-spawned at close.ts:845-846. Credit where due, because it shows the project already knows how to do this: the autonomous review gate is a model of the right shape — a fail-closed CLOSED enumeration of four provably-safe change kinds, explicitly refusing any severity/cost shortcut, with anything unclassifiable excluded by default (src/remediate/review/autonomousGate.ts:26-70). That rigor stops at the door where the blast radius is largest. Recommendation: make the authority per-action rather than per-run and tier it by reversibility — pre_authorized becomes a set of authorized actions rather than a boolean, and the irreversible tier (publish, and arguably push to a protected branch) requires confirmation AT EXECUTION with the actual preview attached, regardless of up-front pre-authorization; the preview material is already computed by collectStagingFiles and generateCommitMessage. Reversible actions keep today's frictionless autonomy.

findings.title: Contract-mismatch failures carry the worker-supplied task_id, misrouting claim clearing and retry-packet derivation
findings.summary: When an arrived result's embedded task_id differs from the assigned task (an explicitly handled case — the mismatch error is generated three lines up), the FailingTask is pushed with the file's bogus id (taskId ?? task.task_id) instead of the assigned identity. Downstream, claimRegistry.clear() then clears a claim under the bogus id — leaving the real task's claim held for the full 20-min lease, and potentially clearing a different live task's claim if the worker stamped a sibling's id — and retry-packet derivation matches result-map entries against the bogus id, so the genuinely failed packet is omitted from retry_packet_ids (or the wrong packet is retried on collision). This contradicts the file's own doctrine that identity is the tool's authority, not the worker's (rebindPacketIdKeyedResult forces all four identity fields for exactly this reason).
evidence: src/audit/cli/mergeAndIngestCommand.ts:518-522 - the code detects taskId !== task.task_id and records it as an error, guaranteeing the result lands in `failing`; line 568 then keys that FailingTask by the worker's taskId rather than the assigned task.task_id.

src/audit/cli/mergeAndIngestCommand.ts:913 - claims are cleared by failing[].task_id; a bogus id clears nothing for the assigned task (its claim stays held to lease expiry, delaying re-dispatch) and can clear an unrelated task's live claim when the stamped id collides with a real task.

src/audit/cli/mergeAndIngestCommand.ts:989-996 - retry_packet_ids is derived by matching failing[].task_id against result-map entries; a non-matching bogus id drops the failed packet from retry-dispatch.json entirely.

src/audit/cli/mergeAndIngestCommand.ts:445-452 - rebindPacketIdKeyedResult states 'Identity is the tool's authority (not the worker's), so force all four from the assigned member's metadata', the principle the failing-path keying violates.

src/audit/cli/mergeAndIngestCommand.ts:754-755 - the ownership gate also looks up ownerTokens[bogusId], which is undefined and fails open, so the misKeyed failure bypasses the peer-claim exclusion before the unconditional clear.

findings.title: COR-a278fbe0 regression assertion path is unreachable — test cannot fail on the regression it locks
findings.summary: The test reads audit_results.jsonl with readJsonFile (a whole-file JSON.parse) and gates its task_id assertions behind Array.isArray(results). audit_results.jsonl is an NDJSON artifact (ndjsonArtifact in src/audit/io/artifacts.ts): with >=2 result lines JSON.parse throws and the .catch(() => null) yields null; with exactly 1 line it parses to an object, not an array. Either way the assertion loop never executes and the test falls through to an unconditional expect(true), so the hardcoded-task_id regression it claims to lock can never fail this test.

findings.title: dc6 rolling-driver tests silently pass (early return) when git init fails — broken environment reads as green
findings.summary: initRepo() returns { ok: false } when 'git init' fails, and all four DC-6 lifecycle/race tests begin with 'if (!ok) return;' — a silent early return with zero assertions. Vitest counts a body that returns early as a PASS, so on a machine with broken/missing git the entire claim-lifecycle, cross-driver, and session-lock-race coverage vacuously greens instead of failing or skipping. This is exactly the failed-review-looks-like-a-clean-review shape the project bans elsewhere (success-shaped empty needs an affirmation); the fix is a loud throw (as cp-node-1-regressions' git helper does) or an explicit skip.

findings.title: Dead condition in populateDeclaredProxyCatalog fixture: String(url).includes("POST") never matches, so the probe path passes only via fail-open
findings.summary: The fetch fixture in 'declared + reachable proxy discovery' guards its /v1/messages probe branch with String(url).includes("POST") — checking the URL string for the HTTP method. findings.title: Declared-but-untyped fields: sources[].no_auth/cost_per_mtok/capability_rank, openai_compatible.no_auth/guided_json, codex.sandbox_mode/model, agy.model, claude_code.prompt_flag escape type validation
findings.summary: Several keys listed in the known-key lists (so they draw no unknown-key warning) are never type-checked. In validateDispatchableSources: `no_auth` (boolean), `cost_per_mtok` (number, the admission router's cost-rank seed), and `capability_rank` (number) — the file's own comment for the string fields explains the hazard ('a non-string here coerces to nonsense downstream rather than failing'). In validateOpenAiCompatibleSection the boolean loop covers only response_format_json and include_referenced_files, omitting `no_auth` and `guided_json`. In validateAgentProviderSection only command/extra_args (and claude_code's skip-permissions) are checked, leaving codex.sandbox_mode (a security-relevant enum passed to `codex exec --sandbox`), codex.model, agy.model, and claude_code.prompt_flag unchecked. Concretely, `no_auth: "true"` (string) passes validation but fails every downstream `=== true` check, so the lane is dropped with the misleading refusal 'source has no api_key_env (declare no_auth: true...)' — telling the operator to do what they believe they already did.

findings.title: decomposeIntent's \band\b split fragments the exact comma-list directive its own contract says must stay whole
findings.summary: The docstring says 'focus on modules A, B, and C' is one directive and that fragmenting it would produce 'spurious unencodable clauses' — but the unconditional split on /\band\b/i cuts that exact example into ['focus on modules A, B,', 'C'] (verified). The trailing fragment 'C' matches no lens/priority/scope signal, so interpretIntent raises a spurious blocking checkpoint question for it — the precise failure mode the no-comma-split rule was designed to prevent. Any natural-language 'and' inside a single directive (including hyphenated forms like 'black-and-white') fragments the same way.

findings.title: Drift-guard test polices two independent 'backlog entry' grammars instead of one shared parser
findings.summary: The test 'shares ONE definition of "a backlog entry" with check-backlog-budget' does not verify a shared definition — it runs check-backlog-budget.mjs --report, regex-scrapes its stdout for per-file entry counts, and asserts count parity against parseBulletEntries from generate-handoff-roadmap.mjs. The two scripts each carry their own entry grammar (parseBulletEntries vs check-backlog-budget's parseEntries built on /^- \*\*/), so this test exists purely to keep two copies of the grammar in sync. The defect is the duplication: extract one shared entry parser both scripts consume, and the drift guard becomes unnecessary. As written the guard is also coupled to the --report output format (a stdout wording change breaks the regex, not the grammar).

The packet's tests-lens guidance and the repo's own convention ('Extract shared logic, don't drift-test it') both mark this shape: single-source the entry grammar and delete the parity check.

findings.title: Every artifact-bundle load re-hashes audit-tools' own 10.3 MB / 2,109-file install to recompute a value that cannot change during a run
findings.summary: loadArtifactBundle unconditionally calls buildToolingManifest() (src/audit/io/artifacts.ts:333). That function recursively walks and reads EVERY byte of six inputs — audit-code.mjs, wrapper/audit-code-wrapper-lib.mjs, package.json, dist/, schemas/, skills/audit-code — serially (one await readFile per file inside a for loop, src/audit/io/toolingManifest.ts:74-87) and folds them into one sha256. Measured on this tree: 2,109 files / 10,317,315 bytes for dist alone, 282-369 ms per call (first call 369 ms, warm repeat 282 ms) against the audit-tools dist actually on disk. For scale, the ENTIRE rest of the load->hash->persist cycle over the live 8.7 MB artifact set measures 122 ms total (parse 27 ms + hash-every-artifact 62 ms + persist-every-artifact 33 ms), so the tool spends 2.5-3x more time hashing ITSELF than handling all of the audit state it exists to manage. The value is a fixed identity of the installed implementation: it cannot change while a run is in flight (a mid-run rebuild of the tool being audited is not a supported state — the artifact even records it as implementation_hash + package_version). Yet loadArtifactBundle has 29 call sites, and nextStepHelpers.ts alone re-loads the whole bundle at 12 separate 'transition' points, so one folded next-step invocation can pay it a dozen times. Two better mechanisms, either of which removes the cost entirely: (a) emit the implementation hash at BUILD time into a generated dist module (one read instead of 2,109 — the identity is a property of the build, not of run-time disk state), or (b) at minimum memoize per process. (b) is a two-line change; (a) is the categorically right one because it also makes the identity stable across concurrent readers and machines instead of re-deriving it from whatever bytes happen to be on disk.

findings.title: Every CI job rebuilds dist from scratch and the test matrix shards by file count rather than duration, so the CI critical path is ~1.7x its achievable floor
findings.summary: Two independent inefficiencies in the same matrix, both measured from the repo's own publish-ci profile record. (b) Duration-blind sharding: vitest --shard partitions by FILE, not by measured duration, and the run's shard times are 205 s / 127 s / 92 s / 60 s. The matrix wall is set by the slowest shard, so the test critical path is 205 s where a duration-balanced split of the same 484 s of work would be ~121 s - a 41% reduction available with no extra runners. findings.title: Extraction opens every source file four to five times and every per-file loop is serial, while the repo's own bounded-concurrency helper is used zero times in the extraction path and its single parallel site is unbounded
findings.summary: There is no shared content pass. fsIntake reads each file in full and throws the bytes away — maybeHashFile does `const content = await readFile(path); return hashContent(content)` (src/audit/extractors/fsIntake.ts:46-53) and the returned manifest carries only {path, size_bytes, hash}. Then graph.ts re-reads every in-scope file into its own function-local fileContents map (src/audit/extractors/graph.ts:507-531) and discards it on return (:543); the per-language analyzers re-read their subsets independently (python.ts:109-112, html.ts:80-83, css.ts:94-97, and typescript.ts:399-400 lets ts.createProgram read them a fourth time); and commentDecomposition re-reads every included file plus every doc file (src/audit/extractors/commentDecomposition.ts:270-271 and :345-346) even though it exposes a readFileText injection seam the only production caller leaves undefined. So one .ts file is opened 4x in-process per extraction and a scanned .md 5x, over 1,210 included files / 13.3 MB measured here. The shape is also serial almost everywhere: the intake walk awaits readdir/stat/hash per entry (fsIntake.ts:77-105) and I measured the same file set at 139 ms read serially vs 39 ms concurrently (3.6x); commentDecomposition, python, html and css all await inside a for-over-files; and the analyzers themselves run strictly one-after-another in a registry for loop (src/audit/orchestrator/graphEnrichmentExecutor.ts:239-256) despite being independent, so a polyglot repo pays the SUM of analyzer times rather than the max. Meanwhile src/shared/concurrency.ts (mapWithConcurrency) exists and is called from exactly two post-ingest sites and zero extraction sites, and the one place extraction IS concurrent — graph.ts:507 — is an unbounded Promise.all over every in-scope file, i.e. the only parallel site is the one that should have a cap. The better arrangement is one bounded read pass that hashes and hands the same buffer to the graph, the analyzers and the comment pass, with mapWithConcurrency as the single primitive: it removes 3 of the 4 passes, replaces the 3.6x-slower serial walk, bounds the fd fan-out, and lets independent analyzers overlap. Worth noting what the incremental tier does and does not cover: the per-file content-keyed reuse in graph.ts:911-916 (via graph_edge_cache) is the right pattern but sits BEHIND the read pass (a 100% cache hit still reads every file) and the analyzer tier has no equivalent — typescript.ts:100 explicitly forces incremental:false/composite:false, so the measured 7.4 s graph-enrichment step rebuilds the whole program whenever it runs at all.

findings.title: Fifteen-plus graph algorithms are hand-rolled with no graph library, including four independent union-find implementations
findings.summary: The core of this product is graph work — import/call/co-change edges, connected components, clustering under size ceilings, cycle detection, topological tiering, transitive staleness propagation — and every algorithm is written from scratch with no graph dependency of any kind. The duplication is measurable. Union-find appears FOUR times: src/audit/orchestrator/unionFind.ts (the named module), a private class in src/shared/decompose/consensus.ts:121-163, inline find/union closures in src/remediate/contractPipeline/cyclicSeamResolution.ts:110-123, and an array-indexed variant in src/audit/orchestrator/partitionTaskGraph.ts:60-71. Cycle detection appears three times in two different styles: DFS-with-rotation-canonical-dedupe in src/audit/extractors/graphSignals.ts:169-212, and three-colour DFS twice, in src/shared/types/obligationLedger.ts:27-63 and src/remediate/validation/contractPipeline.ts:664-698. Alongside those sit a Kahn topological drain, a longest-path memoized tiering pass, greedy agglomerative clustering under two ceilings, connected components over task groups, and DAG inversion with a fixpoint staleness propagation. Two separate hand-rolled bounded-concurrency primitives exist as well — src/shared/concurrency.ts (mapWithConcurrency) and src/shared/quota/slidingWindow.ts (runSlidingWindow) — and the second has no production caller at all, reachable only through re-exports and its own tests, so it is a live instance of the tested-but-unwired class the project tracks manually; it also recurses per completed task, growing a promise chain rather than looping. This is not primarily a correctness complaint — the implementations look careful — it is that the project pays maintenance on a private algorithms library while its own principles say to single-source common logic and prefer extraction over parallel copies. Recommendation: adopt graphology with graphology-components, graphology-dag and graphology-traversal (pure JS, no native build, actively maintained) for components, cycle detection and topological ordering; replace the two concurrency primitives with one, or at minimum delete runSlidingWindow. Retain only the genuinely domain-specific passes — the size-ceiling clustering and the consensus co-association — on top of the library's data structures. Note the interaction with DR-023: a library-provided SCC condensation is exactly the mechanism that would turn the dependency map's five prose acyclicity arguments into a checked property.

findings.title: Grounding resolves the model-supplied cited path with no repo containment, so a finding can be "grounded" against a file outside the audited repo
findings.summary:
TRUST BOUNDARY: `finding.affected_files[].path` is worker output — untrusted data crossing from the LLM into the tool. Every other consumer of a model-supplied path in this codebase routes it through the single containment guard `resolveWithinRoot` (src/shared/io/pathContainment.ts), whose docstring records that this check was reimplemented five times and that "this is the class where that is a security property, not a style preference".

COUNTEREXAMPLE: the grounding verifier does not use it. `verifyFindingGrounding` resolves the cited path as `const absolutePath = isAbsolute(loc.path) ? loc.path : join(repoRoot, loc.path)` (src/shared/validation/findingGrounding.ts:182) — an absolute path is passed through verbatim, and a relative path is `join`ed with no `..` rejection. Verified by running the shipped code: a finding citing `{path: "../../Windows/win.ini", quoted_text: "for 16-bit app support"}` with `repoRoot` set to this repository returned `{"status":"grounded"}`. So the `grounded` bit does not even assert that the cited location is in the repository under audit.

REACHABILITY: this is not filtered upstream. The result validator deliberately keeps such a finding: an `affected_files[].path` outside the declared assigned coverage is pushed as `severity: "warning"` with the message "In-scope findings are retained; this entry is informational only" (src/audit/validation/auditResults.ts:962-974, INV-09/FRIC-010). The path is never containment-checked before it reaches the grounding pass. Note the asymmetry with the sibling normalizer in the same shared module, `normalizeRepoPath` (findingGrounding.ts:46), which is careful about path shape but is used for corpus membership, not for the filesystem read.

RECOMMENDED CHANGE: run the cited path through `resolveWithinRoot(repoRoot, loc.path)` before reading it, and classify a non-contained path as `ungrounded` with an explicit reason ("cited path escapes the audited root") rather than reading it. This is a two-line change at findingGrounding.ts:182 and makes the grounding verdict mean what the report claims it means. Consider also promoting the out-of-scope `affected_files` path from warning to a grounding-disqualifier, so the retained-but-informational entry cannot silently become a confirmed one.

findings.title: isQuotaState accepts entries:null / non-object entry values — corruption class that bypasses the quarantine repair
findings.summary: isQuotaState validates entries with `typeof obj["entries"] === "object"`, which accepts null and arrays, and never checks the shape of individual entry values. A file like {"version":2,"entries":null} therefore passes validation and readQuotaState returns it as a valid QuotaState; the first `state.entries[key]` access then throws a raw TypeError instead of QuotaStateUnavailableError. Because readQuotaStateForUpdate's quarantine repair only catches QuotaStateUnavailableError with kind 'corrupt', this corruption class is never quarantined: every read-modify-write (recordWaveOutcome, slope/ratio recording) fails permanently with an unclassified TypeError and the designed self-heal (quarantine + rebuild from cold state) never engages. A version:1 file with a primitive entry value fails the same way inside the migration loop (`entry.consecutive_429_count ??= 0` throws in strict mode), violating the validate-before-migrate ordering.
evidence: src/shared/quota/state.ts:24-29 - `typeof null === "object"` in JavaScript, so entries:null (and entries:[...]) passes isQuotaState; entry values are never shape-checked.

src/shared/quota/state.ts:149-175 - readQuotaStateForUpdate quarantines only `error instanceof QuotaStateUnavailableError && error.kind === 'corrupt'`; a TypeError thrown later by consumers (e.g. recordWaveOutcomeUnsafe's `state.entries[providerModelKey]` at line 570 on a null entries) propagates unquarantined, so the bad file is never renamed aside and every subsequent write fails identically.

src/shared/quota/state.ts:53-69 - the error class doc states corrupt files are terminal and must be quarantined by the write path; this class of corrupt file defeats that contract because validation passes and the failure surfaces past the guard.

findings.title: Louvain aggregation undercounts self-loop degree, breaking the documented degree-preservation invariant
findings.summary: aggregate() claims each super-node's degree equals the total degree of its members, but buildAdjacency counts the diagonal (self-loop) ONCE in a node's degree. An intra-community pair edge of weight w contributes 2w to member degrees at level N but only w to the super-node's degree (and only w to 2m) at level N+1, so every aggregated level optimizes a distorted modularity: communities with intra mass look 'lighter' than they are, biasing coarse levels toward over-merging. For the multilevel method to be exact, a self-loop must contribute twice its weight to the node's degree (standard Louvain convention).

degree = Σ over incident edge weights (diagonal counted once)

evidence: src/shared/decompose/modularity.ts:79 - self-loop weight added once to the diagonal; degree is later computed as the plain row sum, so the diagonal counts once.

findings.title: madge was rejected for a fixable packaging reason and replaced with a regex cycle detector that is blind to the project's own primary import form
findings.summary: tests/audit/helpers/importCycles.mjs (135 lines) states its own provenance: it replaced an npx madge --circular guard because madge was not a declared dependency (fetched on demand by npx), so the guard was network/cache-dependent and flaky and silently passed when madge failed to resolve. Every one of those complaints is about the INVOCATION, not the library — the fix is to declare it as a devDependency. What replaced it is strictly weaker in a way that matters here: the detector explicitly follows only relative specifiers, on the reasoning that bare package specifiers are external and cannot close an in-repo cycle — but in this repo the bare specifier audit-tools/shared IS an in-repo import, used 279 times in src/audit and 113 times in src/remediate and aliased back to src/shared in vitest.config.ts. So no cycle that passes through audit-tools/shared is detectable, which means no audit-to-shared or remediate-to-shared cycle is detectable at all, and shared is the layer both orchestrators depend on — precisely where a cycle would hurt. It is also blind to the 8 dynamic import() sites in src/ and to tsconfig path aliases generally. The tell that this is a real gap rather than a theoretical one: the structural analysis of this repo reports nine dependency cycles, all of them intra-directory (src/shared/providers/*, src/shared/quota/*, src/remediate/contractPipeline/*, src/remediate/state/*) — exactly the subset a relative-only walker can see — while DR-015 identifies a genuine quota-to-providers runtime cycle through the barrel that this guard cannot reach. Recommendation: declare dependency-cruiser as a devDependency and use it for both jobs. It resolves through tsconfig (so the audit-tools/shared alias is followed), understands dynamic and type-only imports, and — the larger win — expresses architectural boundary rules as declarative forbidden config, which would let several bespoke INV-* layering tests and the loop-core pattern list from DR-029 collapse into data rather than prose.

findings.title: MCP was built as a 992-line server, retired with no recorded rationale, and replaced by ~5,250 lines of bespoke host adapters — with four live residues still in the tree
findings.summary: This project's entire host surface is: write files into host-specific config locations, then be invoked as a shell command. wrapper/audit-code-wrapper-install-hosts.mjs and its remediate twin maintain four repo-local host descriptors (codex, opencode, vscode, antigravity) and postinstall adds five global targets, giving nine artifact families across markdown, markdown-with-YAML-frontmatter, TOML, JSON manifest and deep-merged JSON — roughly 5,250 production lines, about 2,400 of them near-verbatim audit/remediate duplication, guarded by another ~2,550 lines of drift tests. The single best part is real and worth keeping: every asset renders from ONE canonical loader body through renderHostAsset in src/shared/hostAssets.ts, so the per-format writers are thin. The finding is not 'adopt MCP' — it is that the decision justifying this entire layer is unrecoverable. Commit a80cb74f (2026-06-03) deleted a 992-line stdio MCP server exposing start_audit/get_status/continue_audit, plus the Claude Desktop registration, the global launcher and the OpenCode mcp.auditor entry, and its own message says it pruned MCP mentions from CLAUDE.md and docs. Searching docs/, spec/, README.md, CLAUDE.md and the whole backlog turns up no design note, no retired-decision record and no ADR for the retirement; the only rationale anywhere is that commit message. Meanwhile the absence is enforced by roughly eight negative guard tests and by runtime throws in the installers. For a project whose documentation philosophy is that docs capture durable concepts, and which keeps a standing durable-traps.md precisely so decisions are not relitigated, deleting the reasoning for retiring the cross-vendor host-integration standard — while every host it targets has since shipped MCP support — means the tradeoff cannot be re-examined, only re-discovered. Four residues also remain live and should be cleaned regardless: wrapper/audit-code-wrapper-lib.mjs still branches on an mcp argv and advertises in --help that mcp starts the local stdio MCP server, for a command src/audit/cli.ts no longer implements; the step contract still ships allowed_mcp_tools (src/audit/cli/steps.ts) populated in src/audit/cli/nextStepCommand.ts with auditor_continue_audit/auditor_merge_and_ingest — names of deleted tools — covered by PASSING contract tests, so a dead field reads as a live feature; skills/audit-code/SKILL.md still promises shared MCP setup guidance; and scripts/audit/postinstall.mjs keeps allowlist entries for run-mcp-server.mjs plus a recovery message telling the operator to add the mcp.auditor entry that install itself now rejects. Recommendation: write the retirement rationale into a durable record so the choice is auditable, and delete the four residues atomically.

findings.title: mergePartialTerminals drops empty_grant_cause on every merge, and a reset-less structural pause annexes real pool exhaustion
findings.summary: mergePartialTerminals rebuilds the merged terminal from only reason/stranded_ids/earliest_reset_at, so the empty_grant_cause field ('no_capable_pool' etc.) never survives a two-terminal merge — even when BOTH inputs are structural no_capable_pool pauses. The engine's getTerminal deliberately emits structural strands as quota_paused + empty_grant_cause:'no_capable_pool' with NO reset; because that reason string is 'quota_paused', the merge's paused-wins preference also converts a genuine empty_pool terminal from another sub-wave into a bare 'quota_paused' with neither reset nor cause — inverting the engine's own doctrine that dead pools are the fact the operator must act on first (rollingDispatch.ts:2090-2096), and starving the downstream consumer that branches on the cause (remediate nextStep reads terminal.empty_grant_cause to avoid telling the operator to wait for a reset no reset can clear).
evidence: src/shared/dispatch/unifiedRolling.ts:45-66 - the merged object literal carries only reason, stranded_ids, and (conditionally) earliest_reset_at; empty_grant_cause is silently dropped whenever prior and next are both non-null.

src/shared/quota/capacity.ts:83 - empty_grant_cause is an explicit field of PartialCompletionTerminal ('no_capable_pool' means a structural fit mismatch NO reset can clear, so the pause step must not tell the operator to wait for one).
src/remediate/steps/nextStep.ts:5147 - the merged terminal's consumer reads terminal.empty_grant_cause and threads it into buildQuotaPausedStep; after any multi-terminal drive it always sees null.

findings.title: No timeout on any analyzer spawn — a hung external tool blocks the whole synchronous engine indefinitely
findings.summary: The default runner is runTracked(argv, { cwd }) with no timeout option, and runTracked passes timeout straight through to spawnSync (undefined = wait forever). The engine is fully synchronous, so a wedged tool — semgrep on a huge repo, osv-scanner waiting on its network API, an npx install stalled on a dead registry connection, or even a runner --version probe that hangs — blocks the entire audit next-step with no recovery path. The degrade-to-empty design covers failures, not hangs.

findings.title: npm install rewrites the consuming repo's .gitignore and shells out to gh to guess repository visibility
findings.summary: Installing the package mutates the user's repository. scripts/postinstall.mjs:31 calls manageArtifactGitignore(), which resolves INIT_CWD as the consuming repo root and writes a marker-delimited managed block into that repo's .gitignore (src/shared/io/gitignoreArtifacts.ts:143-199). To decide the block's contents it runs a four-tier visibility-authority chain: an environment variable, then a committed .audit-tools-visibility marker file, then gh repo view --json isPrivate — a GitHub CLI subprocess during npm install (:202-232). That is 351 lines plus a network-capable shell-out, and the decision it buys is whether one output file is tracked by default. Three things make this a poor trade regardless of how carefully it degrades. A postinstall script writing to a file the user's VCS tracks is surprising in a way no amount of idempotency fixes — it will show up as an unexplained diff. Inferring intent from repository visibility is a guess about a policy question the user is better placed to answer, and a wrong guess in the private-to-public direction is exactly the leak the feature exists to prevent. And an npm install that invokes gh will behave differently in CI, in a container, and offline, for reasons unrelated to installing a package. Recommendation: delete the inference. Always ignore the runtime tree (.audit-tools/audit/, .audit-tools/remediation/) since it is machine state nobody wants committed, never touch .gitignore for the deliverables, and document in the README the one line a user adds if they want audit-report.md tracked. That removes 351 lines, a subprocess, an environment variable, a marker file, and a class of surprise, and hands a policy decision back to the person who owns it. Note DR-020: this file also runs on every consumer machine and is outside every tsconfig.

findings.title: OS-agnosticism is a declared invariant that no gate ever tests: all five CI jobs are ubuntu-latest, so every Windows and macOS code path is verified only by the maintainer's own machine
findings.summary: Every other stated invariant in this project is enforced mechanically - guard reach is a reconciled registry, doc paths are generated-and-checked, loop-core review is a tree-bound attestation - but 'everything-agnostic by default, OS/platform-agnostic specifically' rests entirely on the maintainer happening to develop on Windows. Verified exhaustively: runs-on appears 5 times across the three workflows and is ubuntu-latest every time, and a case-insensitive grep for windows, macos or darwin across .github/workflows returns zero hits. So the whole win32 branch - resolveWindowsShimSpawnCommand and the .cmd/.ps1 shim resolution, the process.platform === 'win32' bin-path branches in both packaged smokes, the npm.cmd spawn wrapper, CRLF handling and path-separator normalization - is never exercised by any gate, and darwin is never exercised at all. This is the repo's own recorded trap 'Windows-local green != Linux-CI green' running in both directions at once: a Linux-only regression is caught locally, a Windows-only or macOS-only regression is caught by nobody, and the tree ships two published bins plus a consumer postinstall that runs on all three. A strategy: [ubuntu-latest, windows-latest, macos-latest] matrix on the existing suite job is a near-zero-maintenance change that converts the project's most broadly-claimed invariant from an assertion into a gate. Scoping it to one shard or one Node line on the non-Linux legs keeps the added minutes small while still making the platform-specific branches load-bearing in CI.

findings.title: Packet graph context is rebuilt by a full sweep of the whole edge set once per packet, and the two order-only callers build the entire annotated packetization only to throw every packet away
findings.summary: buildReviewPackets does its graph work correctly ONCE and then undoes that discipline per packet. collectGraphEdges (reviewPackets.ts:475), buildPlanningGraphEdges (:478) and mergeGraphConnectedGroups (:489) each run a single time over the whole edge set, but the emit loop (:500-518) then calls buildPacket PER PACKET, and every buildPacket calls buildPacketGraphContext (:390), which iterates the ENTIRE planningGraphEdges array (reviewPacketGraphContext.ts:81) and, via packetEntrypoints (:120), filters the entire graphs.routes array as well. So the payload build is O(packets x edges) sitting behind a clustering pass that is already O(edges). Measured against this repo's own artifacts (collectGraphEdges returns 6,614 concrete edges from the 3.37 MB graph_bundle.json): buildReviewPackets over 141 synthetic tasks on real repo paths costs 861 ms, over 468 tasks 2,335 ms; the identical call with no graphBundle supplied costs 32 ms and 35 ms, so ~98.5% of packetization time is the per-packet graph payload. I prototyped the fix and measured it: building one endpoint->edges adjacency index ONCE and visiting only the edges incident to each packet's own files produces byte-identical internal/boundary counts (11,724 both ways) and drops the kernel from 90.6 ms to 3.6 ms for 100 packets over the 6,614 edges - 25x. The module already exports exactly this primitive, buildGraphDegreeIndex (reviewPacketGraph.ts:24), and buildPacketGraphContext does not use it. Second, independent half: orderTasksForPacketReview (reviewPackets.ts:599) is `buildReviewPackets(tasks, options).flatMap(...)` (:604) - it pays the whole per-packet payload and then reduces the packets to a task-id list. That ordering cannot depend on the payload: makeComparePackets (:158) sorts on priority -> continuity -> task count -> packet_id and reads no graph field. It is called from dispatch.ts:376 and from buildPendingAuditTasks (packetFilter.ts:59, :73), whose five callers are dispatch.ts:272, mergeAndIngestCommand.ts:958, reviewRun.ts:135, nextStepHelpers.ts:2434 and nextStepHelpers.ts:2640 - and the last two need no ordering at all (2434 consumes only {task_id, token_estimate}; 2640, the unconditional next-step preamble, consumes only the file_line_counts key set). findings.title: Provider reach is re-probed by blocking process spawn twice per next-step because the resolver's own docblock prices ambient resolution as 'one small JSON read' - and the PATH probe itself is implemented twice with different semantics
findings.summary: resolveSessionConfig's docblock states the cost model that made the duplication invisible: 'It stays cheap (one small JSON read, and only on the descriptor-present path)' (resolveSessionConfig.ts:85-88). The JSON read is not the cost. When a descriptor omits `sources` it calls resolveAmbientSources (:120), which loops every declared source through verifySourceReach (auditorSources.ts:465, loop at :615); for the codex/opencode/agy CLI transports that is a synchronous spawnSync of `where`/`which` (providerPathGuard.ts:29-38) and for a keyless openai-compatible source it is an HTTP liveness probe. Measured on this box: 66.5 ms per `where` probe (10 probes = 665 ms; an immediate repeat of the same 10 = 628 ms, i.e. no memoization anywhere), and it is spawnSync, so it blocks the loop. probeCommandOnPath's own comment already says it 'runs on every provider discovery, so it is the most frequent offender' - the observation was made and then not acted on. One `next-step` pays it twice over: nextStepCommand.ts:426 loadSessionConfig then :532 resolveSessionConfig, and later in the SAME invocation semanticReviewStep.ts:108-110 does `resolveSessionConfig(await loadSessionConfig(artifactsDir), params.descriptor)` again, whose comment (:105-107) frames the re-load as deliberate freshness ('freshly-loaded (and re-validated, fail-closed)'). So per invocation: 2 reads of session-config.json, 2 full runs of the 1,030-line validateRepoSessionIntent over identical bytes, 2 declaration-file reads, and 2 x N blocking PATH spawns plus 2 x M network probes for N CLI and M keyless sources. Nothing is cached at any layer - sessionConfigStore constructs a fresh store per call (supervisor/sessionConfig.ts:35) and resolveAmbientSources holds no state - even though the repo memoizes exactly this class of environment fact elsewhere (modelStatics.ts's module-level snapshot cache, detectRepoConventionsCache). Two changes: resolve reach ONCE per process and thread the result (this does not fight the escalation design - both resolutions happen seconds apart inside one process, so the second cannot observe a change the first missed, and cross-invocation re-probing is untouched), and collapse the two PATH-probe implementations into one: providerPathGuard.ts:29 is sync spawnSync with no timeout and a test-injection hook, while audit/validation/sessionConfig.ts:28 is a second, module-private async execFile probe with a 5 s timeout and no hook - the same `where`/`which` check written twice with divergent timeout and testability semantics. Distinct from SC-008: that is a content hash recomputed over the tool's own install bytes; this is duplicated blocking subprocess and network probing driven by a docblock that misprices its own cost, plus a duplicated probe implementation.

findings.title: Quota and rate-limit classification depends on regex-matching vendor PROSE, because nine of ten providers are CLI subprocesses with no structured error channel
findings.summary: The load-bearing assumption behind the whole quota subsystem is that a vendor CLI's human-readable stderr is a stable machine interface. src/shared/quota/errorParsing.ts (425 lines) classifies dispatch failures by matching English against captured output: RATE_LIMIT_PATTERNS, USAGE_LIMIT_PATTERNS, CREDIT_EXHAUSTION_PATTERNS, and a RESET_INDICATOR_PATTERN that vetoes a credit match when the prose sounds transient. The comments are candid that this is load-bearing and fragile — the veto exists because permanently sinking a pool that would have recovered is worse than the bug it fixes. None of it would be necessary with a structured channel: HTTP gives 429 plus Retry-After as a standard, and every vendor emits machine-readable error codes in the response body. The reason it is necessary is architectural and worth naming as such: of the ten entries in PROVIDER_NAMES, nine dispatch by spawning a subprocess (claude, codex, opencode, agy, plus the template-driven vscode-task/antigravity/worker-command/subprocess-template and the proxied claude-worker), and exactly one — openai-compatible — speaks HTTP. So the single provider with access to status codes and structured bodies is the exception, and the substrate is built for the majority case. Two consequences follow. First, a vendor rewording a message silently degrades a retryable pause into a misclassified permanent failure or vice versa, with no compile-time or test-time signal — the patterns can only be validated against strings someone once observed. Second, the same transport choice is why quota discovery needs seven bespoke source modules (claudeOAuthQuotaSource, codexQuotaSource, copilotQuotaSource, openCodeQuotaSource, antigravityQuotaSource, hostSessionQuotaSource, httpQuotaSource) scraping credential stores and undocumented endpoints. Recommendation: treat HTTP as the preferred transport wherever a vendor offers one and reserve CLI spawning for hosts that genuinely have no API, so structured status and Retry-After become the primary classification path and prose matching degrades to a last-resort fallback; and make prose classification declared, versioned data with recorded provenance per pattern (which vendor, which observed message, which date) rather than inline literals, so staleness is auditable. Note the project already reasons well about HTTP transport correctness in src/shared/providers/openAiCompatibleProvider.ts, where a documented UND_ERR_HEADERS_TIMEOUT bug drove a per-launch undici Agent with explicit deadlines — evidence the HTTP path is the better-instrumented one.

findings.title: Rotated OAuth credential file rewritten without restrictive permissions
findings.summary: writeCredentialsAtomic rewrites ~/.claude/.credentials.json (containing the live OAuth access AND refresh tokens) via writeFileSync with no mode option, so on POSIX the refreshed credential file (and the transient .tmp file) is created with umask-default permissions (typically 0644, world-readable) instead of the 0600 the CLI-created credential file carries. findings.title: The "extractors emit stable, content-derived array order" invariant has no mechanical guard, and `flows.ts` already contradicts itself between its build and merge paths
findings.summary:
INFERRED CONTRACT: stated explicitly in CLAUDE.md — "Any artifact array field must be ordered by a stable key derived from content (e.g. path-sort), never filesystem / `readdir` / iteration order. `stableStringify` preserves array order, so an incidentally-ordered array silently churns the artifact's content hash on every re-extraction → cascades phantom staleness down the dependency DAG → redundant (expensive) downstream LLM re-runs." The project also states that durable traps must be MECHANICALLY enforced rather than remembered, and that a trap enforceable as a contract test earns deletion from the backlog.

COUNTEREXAMPLE: this one is enforced only by prose. `stableStringify` does preserve array order (src/shared/stableStringify.ts:21), so the hash consequence is real; but there is no property test, no check script, and no hook. tests/audit/audit-extractors-invariants.test.ts covers edge shape, cycle detection, regex hangs, ignore files and disposition guards — no sortedness invariant; nothing under `scripts/` or `.claude/hooks/` addresses array order; coverage is only per-artifact spot assertions in unrelated tests. Meanwhile the invariant is already violated in spirit inside a single file: `extractCriticalFlows` returns `dedupeFlows(flows)` with NO sort (src/audit/extractors/flows.ts:143-147), while the host-fallback merge path in the SAME file sorts by id — `[...byId.values()].sort((a, b) => a.id.localeCompare(b.id))` (flows.ts:211). So `critical_flows.json.flows[]` is id-sorted when produced by the merge and push-ordered when produced by the primary build: the same logical artifact has two orderings, and a run that takes the fallback path changes the array order — and hence the content hash — without any semantic change. `surface_manifest.json.surfaces[]` (src/audit/extractors/surfaces.ts:69) and `risk_register.json.items[]` (src/audit/extractors/risk.ts) are likewise emitted in push order; they are stable today only because they transitively inherit the deliberately path-sorted `repo_manifest.files` (src/audit/extractors/fileInventory.ts:45-55), which makes the ordering load-bearing at a distance and one input-order change away from firing.

RECOMMENDED CHANGE: convert the prose into a test, then delete the prose obligation. A single cross-extractor property test can assert it generically — for each artifact array field with an id/path-like key, re-run the extractor over a shuffled input file order and assert byte-identical `stableStringify` output. That catches the whole class rather than the named instances. Independently, make the two `critical_flows` producers agree by sorting at the primary build site (the cheapest correct fix, since the merge path already sorts).

findings.title: The "per-run" analyzer consent token is a presence check on persisted config, so consent is granted permanently on first write and any non-blank string unlocks every gated tool
findings.summary:
INFERRED CONTRACT: `admitSpawn` is documented as the "Single subprocess-SPAWN admission chokepoint" where "EVERY other candidate — including `permanent`/`ephemeral` pre-installed tools — requires the per-run consent token (CE-005)" (src/audit/extractors/analyzers/acquisitionEngine.ts:210-215). CLAUDE.md describes it as "a mechanical run-safety gate + curated default set + first-use consent". "Per-run" implies the consent is scoped to one run.

COUNTEREXAMPLE: nothing binds the token to a run. The check is `if (consentToken && consentToken.trim().length > 0) return undefined;` (acquisitionEngine.ts:223) — presence only. There is no expected value, no run id, no nonce, no expiry, and no comparison of any kind anywhere in the tree (no `timingSafeEqual`, no constant to compare against). Verified by running the shipped code: `"x"`, `"no"`, `"false"`, and `"   y"` each admit a `defaultRun: false` candidate. The token's only source is the persisted `session-config.json` (`intent.external_acquisition?.consent_token`, src/audit/cli/nextStepCommand.ts:580) — there is no CLI flag — and the only config mutator spreads the base record verbatim (`persistAnalyzerSettings`, src/audit/supervisor/sessionConfig.ts:126-129), so once written the token survives every subsequent run. The effective scope is therefore per-repo-forever, not per-run: the gate answers "has anyone ever written a non-blank string into this file", which is a persisted boolean, not a consent decision attached to the run being admitted.

SCOPE NOTE: this is deliberately NOT a report of the strip/redact-before-persist item, which CLAUDE.md and docs/backlog/forward-tracks.md already track as a known unimplemented forward constraint. The gap here is the run-scoping and verification semantics of the gate itself, which is not tracked.

RECOMMENDED CHANGE: make the token mean what its name says. Bind it to the run — mint it per run (or require it to carry the current `run_id`) and have `admitSpawn` verify that binding rather than testing for non-blankness, so a token persisted by an earlier run does not admit a later one. If the intended semantics really are "the operator opted this repo in once", then rename the field and the docstring to say so (`external_acquisition.opt_in: true`), because a value-carrying field named `consent_token` that is never compared will keep reading as a verified secret to future maintainers.
