findings.title: The always-on profiling ledger and the flake baseline are both scope-blind: a one-file dev run overwrites the suite baseline because the ledger key derives from `--shard` alone, so 83% of the vitest record is dev noise
findings.summary: The profiling stack is deliberately always-on so "a time regression is visible without anyone remembering to enable it" (scripts/shared/profile.mjs:9-10), but the ledger identity discards the one dimension that decides whether two records are comparable: how much of the suite ran. `shardSuffix(argv)` (scripts/shared/vitestShard.mjs:6-12) keys ONLY on `--shard`; both writers — the gate (scripts/shared/run-vitest-gate.mjs:70) and the in-process reporter (scripts/shared/vitest-timing-reporter.mjs:478) — compose the name as `vitest${shardSuffix(...)}`, so `npx vitest run tests/audit/one.test.ts` and a full-suite `npm test` (the ledger's own widest record is 565 files) write the same `vitest-latest.json` and append to the same `vitest-history.ndjson`. Measured on the live ledger: 2,225 records over three weeks, of which 1,845 (82.9%) are runs of <=11 files and only 257 (11.6%) exceed 300 files; the fileCount histogram peaks at 1 (938 records). `vitest-latest.json` — the snapshot a regression check would read — currently holds a 3-file run (totalMs 2,268, fileCount 3), as do the three most recent history lines. The only full-suite measurement present in the whole directory is `vitest-shard4of4-latest.json`, dated 2026-07-16 (13 days stale), and its two slowest entries (`tests/audit/audit-code-completion.test.mjs`, `tests/audit/audit-code-wrapper.test.mjs`) no longer exist under those names — they were converted to `.ts`. So the evidence base this very review round mined for two earlier findings has no current suite baseline and no way to filter for one. The same blindness reaches the flake record: `loadClassOf` (vitest-timing-reporter.mjs:170-171) collapses scope to a binary — `solo` iff fileCount === 1 — so a 3-file run on 16 workers is classified `parallel` exactly like a full-suite run, and `evidenceSlot` (:206-209) files a failure from either as `failedParallel`, i.e. "failed under load". Three files on sixteen workers has essentially no contention, so that record admits a near-solo failure as contention evidence, which is the same direction the project explicitly refuses to move on guesses. Both writers already hold the number: `perFile.length` at reporter:479 and `files.length` at :375. The fix is one derivation, in the module that already exists to stop these two writers drifting: extend `vitestShard.mjs` to a `ledgerScope(argv, fileCount)` that separates a full-suite run from a filtered one (distinct ledger basename, or a `scope`/`selectedFraction` field the history can be filtered on), and let the load class carry the selected fraction instead of a fileCount>1 boolean. Cheap, mechanical, and it restores a trendable suite baseline plus a flake record that can tell contention from code.

findings.title: The default answer to two places computing the same thing is a parity test — 26 of them — against the project's own prefer-extraction rule
findings.summary: The stated rule (project-philosophy B3) is to prefer extraction over drift tests: single-source two copies instead of guarding them, and make drift impossible. In practice the tree carries 26 test files whose named purpose is parity/sync/drift/lockstep guarding, plus 23 in-source comments of the form keep-in-lockstep or must-stay-in-sync. The tests' own docstrings record the defects the duplication caused, which is the strongest available argument that extraction rather than guarding is the fix: tests/audit/dispatch-entrypoint-parity.test.ts opens by stating that prepare-dispatch and quota both resolve WHICH driver the fan-out is keyed to and both load the same session-config.json to do it, then lists two bugs — the same fail-open try/catch existing in both copies, and the two copies resolving the host model differently so the preview reported one form while the real dispatch keyed another; tests/audit/executor-registry-sync.test.ts names an obligation silently dropped from one of four copies (DR-011); and tests/audit/seam-dependency-map-executor-writeset-parity.test.ts recovers executor write-sets by reading executor module source TEXT to compare against the dependency map — a relation that should be data being re-derived by text-scraping inside a test. The cleanest extractable instance is the provider layer, where the mode axis and the provider axis were multiplied out into files instead of crossed as data: src/audit/providers/ and src/remediate/providers/ are a 2x5 grid of near-identical wrappers (~300 lines total) whose entire information content is six scalars — per mode, a session-config path, a slash command, and a skip-permissions default. The two agyProvider.ts files differ only in those three values, and so do the two claudeCodeProvider.ts files. The axes do not compose (adding a provider costs two new files, adding a mode costs five) and tests/audit/providers-remediation.test.ts plus tests/remediate/providers.test.ts exist to keep the grid honest. One OrchestratorProfile record per mode plus the existing shared provider classes replaces the whole grid and the parity tests with it. Recommendation: treat a new parity test as a design smell requiring justification, and adopt the standing rule that a property expressible as 'these two must agree' is a request to delete one of them.

findings.title: The design-review fan-out renders a 47-51 KB identical corpus 6 times and puts the only varying lines FIRST, so the fan-out has no cacheable prompt prefix
findings.summary: renderConceptualPerspectivePrompt composes the prompt as [title with perspective name, 'one of N reviewers' line, '## Your perspective: <name>', perspective.lens, ...] and only THEN calls renderSharedStructuralContext(bundle, maxUnits). Measured on this run's own emitted prompts: the five conceptual perspective prompts are 54,529-54,586 bytes each and differ at exactly three lines - 1, 5 and 7 - so ~51 KB (96%) of every prompt is byte-identical; 134 of the 205 conceptual lines (~47 KB) are also byte-identical with design-review-contract-prompt.md, which calls the same renderSharedStructuralContext. So one corpus is rendered six times per review phase. Because provider prompt caching is PREFIX-keyed and the divergence sits at line 1, the six dispatches share a zero-length common prefix and none of that corpus is cache-eligible. Move the perspective identity block to AFTER renderSharedStructuralContext (into the trailing critique-instructions/output-format section, where the per-perspective mandate already lives) and the corpus becomes a single shared prefix across all six dispatches - ~96% of the fan-out's input tokens become cache-eligible with no change to what any reviewer is told. Same one-line reordering also makes the corpus reusable across challenge rounds, which re-render it again per round.

findings.title: The doc system's load-bearing assumption is a reader who traverses five homes — and its one orienting map is declared to lose
findings.summary: docs/project-philosophy.md is the one document that gives the whole picture, and its own lines 7-8 disqualify it: it does not replace the canonical homes, and when the map and a home disagree, the home wins. The orienting read is non-authoritative by construction. To resolve an actual rule a reader may need CLAUDE.md, plus spec/, plus project memory (which lives OUTSIDE the repo under the host's per-project store), plus docs/backlog/. Individual routing lines make the traversal explicit, sending the reader to memory for the ask/defer pair, noting that prefer-extraction-over-drift-tests is not yet in CLAUDE.md, and marking other rules memory-only. CLAUDE.md is 288 lines but 35.8 KB because the lines are enormous: the durable-traps-are-mechanically-enforced bullet runs 37 lines and names nine hooks inline, and the end-of-sprint-cleanup bullet is a single ~900-word paragraph with seven numbered sub-clauses and four routing destinations. These are reference tables wearing bullet costumes; no reader parses a 900-word bullet — they skim it and miss a clause. Meanwhile the governance is heavy and pointed at a different property: of the 23 verify legs, the eleven documentation gates (DR-019) all measure CONSISTENCY, and none measures whether anything can be understood. The project even proves it knows how to gate for readability — check:backlog-budget exists specifically because backlog entries grew past navigability — but that gate was never pointed at CLAUDE.md, which is read far more often. What breaks if the assumption is wrong: a fresh agent or engineer on a context budget will not traverse five homes; it will read the map — the doc declared to lose — and act on it. Under the project's own north star that the tool must be trustworthy even when the reader is weak, a documentation set that only works for a reader who does the full traversal is the same latent failure mode the code is not allowed to have. Recommendation: pick ONE authoritative orientation document and let it win, demoting the others to detail references rather than co-authorities; point the existing budget-gate mechanism at CLAUDE.md with a per-bullet line cap, forcing the 37-line and 900-word bullets to become the tables they already are.

findings.title: The execution order is pure data, but the only readable account of it is hand-written and explicitly disclaimed
findings.summary: README.md:138-166 walks the audit pipeline in eight numbered steps — the single most useful page in the repo for a newcomer — and then retracts itself: the numbering is a conceptual grouping rather than the literal execution sequence, and the authoritative order is the PRIORITY array in src/audit/orchestrator/nextStep.ts. README.md:188-189 does the same for remediate. So the only readable description of what the tool does is, by its own admission, not what the tool does, and the authoritative version is a source array a non-developer will never open. This is a solved problem in this very repo: PRIORITY is a flat string array, EXECUTOR_REGISTRY is pure data and already carries kind: deterministic | host_delegation — exactly the 'does this pause and ask me something' distinction a reader wants — and the registry-to-priority mapping is asserted 1:1 at module load. Everything needed to generate an accurate ordered walkthrough is machine-readable today, and the repo already owns the generator pattern: check:philosophy-brief generates the README's Philosophy block from docs/project-philosophy.md and fails the build on drift. By the project's own standard this is the worst of the three available options — prefer-extraction-over-drift-tests says single-source it, and the current state is neither single-sourced nor drift-tested but a hand-written narrative kept honest by a disclaimer, which is the thing the philosophy explicitly bans (a drift test made of memory). Recommendation: generate the step-by-step section from PRIORITY plus EXECUTOR_REGISTRY (and the remediate ladders after DR-011), gated the same way as the philosophy brief, and add a one-line human blurb per obligation id in the registry so the description lives next to the thing it describes and cannot drift. Then delete both disclaimers, because the numbering becomes the real order.

findings.title: The git-history miner's 1,000-commit default hides 61% of change hotspots and 91% of the bus-factor signal on this repo, and unlike the other bound it does not record that it truncated
findings.summary: `mineGitHistory` caps the log walk at `DEFAULT_MAX_COMMITS = 1000` (src/shared/git.ts:169) and the audit extractor calls it with no options (src/audit/extractors/gitHistory.ts:83), so the cap always binds. This repo has 2,092 non-merge commits, so the mine sees 47.8% of its own history. Measured by re-running the miner's exact argv (`git log --use-mailmap --no-merges --name-only --format=%H%x00%aN`) at max-count=1000 versus full history and re-deriving the aggregates against the extractor's own thresholds: files reaching `CHURN_HOTSPOT_FLOOR = 8` (gitHistory.ts:48) fall from 307 to 120 — the cap hides 61% of the change hotspots; files reaching `BROAD_AUTHORSHIP_FLOOR = 4` (:46) fall from 35 to 3 — 91% of the bus-factor signal is erased; files with any churn at all fall from 2,981 to 1,561. Individual counts are halved (docs/backlog.md 578 -> 348, package-lock.json 357 -> 129), which matters because both floors are ABSOLUTE counts applied to a window-relative sample: the same file crosses or misses `change_hotspot` depending purely on how much history was scanned. Those two signals are merged into the risk register (`gitHistoryRiskSignals`, gitHistory.ts:130-156) and therefore steer audit-task prioritisation. What the cap buys is measurable and small: the same single spawn either way, 387 ms full-history versus 217 ms capped on this repo — 170 ms, against an audit run measured in minutes. And the artifact already has the precedent for declaring its own bound: `skipped_cochange_commits` is carried precisely so a consumer knows the O(files^2) pair bound bit (src/shared/git.ts:141-151, 291-293), while the commit-window truncation — the bound that actually bit here — is recorded nowhere, so a downstream reader cannot tell a genuinely low-churn file from an unseen one. Better: scale the window to the repo (walk full history, or bound on log BYTES rather than a fixed commit count, since cost tracks output size not commits) and emit the window actually scanned plus a `truncated_at_commits` field alongside the existing skip counter, so the one bound that is invisible becomes as declared as the one that already is.

findings.title: The learned output/input ratio is an end-to-end dead leg: no production caller writes it, the sole production reader never asks for it, and `reconcile(leaseId)` cannot close the loop the spec of record claims
findings.summary: spec/dispatch-quota.md:357-358 states the design as fact: reservations use the "learned empirical output/input ratio once completions have measured it. On completion the lease reconciles against actual (input + output) tokens, which updates the learned ratio." No part of that loop is wired, verified three ways. (a) NO WRITER: `recordOutputRatioObservation` (src/shared/quota/state.ts:311) and `foldOutputRatioObservation` (:278) have zero production callers — grep across src/, scripts/ and tests/ returns exactly two hits outside their own module, `src/shared/index.ts:1037` (a re-export) and `tests/shared/packet-cost-output-ratio.test.ts` (the only thing that ever calls them). (b) NO READER: the sole production call site of the cost function is `src/shared/dispatch/admissionLoop.ts:911`, and it passes `{ inputEstimate, declaredOutputCap }` only — never `learnedRatio`, so the `if (ratio !== null) return inputEstimate * ratio` branch at src/shared/quota/packetCost.ts:48 is unreachable in a real run and every reservation permanently takes the cold-start `declaredOutputCap` path at :50. The only suppliers of `learnedRatio` anywhere are that same test file and tests/shared/reservation-dispatch-overshoot.test.ts. (c) THE LOOP IS UNCLOSEABLE AS SHAPED: `ReservationLedger.reconcile(leaseId)` (src/shared/quota/reservationLedger.ts:372) takes a lease id and nothing else, so the completion path structurally has no actual-token counts to fold — the feedback edge the spec and the packetCost.ts:58 docblock both describe has no data path. Meanwhile the plumbing reads as live: `output_per_input` is declared on `QuotaStateEntry` (src/shared/quota/types.ts:83), deliberately preserved by `normalizeEntry` (state.ts:210), and propagated across account keys (src/shared/quota/accountId.ts:162). Provenance: the feature landed as commit 5e0a4479 "add reservation ledger + output-envelope cost substrate (admission control 1/3)" — step 1 of 3 shipped, the learning step never did, and the spec was written as if it had. This is the tested-but-unwired class CLAUDE.md says is swept by periodic manual audit, and knip default-mode cannot see it precisely because a test consumes every symbol. Two honest endpoints, both better than today: wire it (thread actual input+output usage into `reconcile`, fold the ratio, and read `output_per_input[lens]` at admission — the reservation then tracks measured reality instead of a flat cap, which is the whole reason the substrate exists), or delete the learner, the `output_per_input` field, its `normalizeEntry`/`accountId` propagation and its test, and correct spec/dispatch-quota.md to say reservations use the declared cap. What must not persist is a spec and three docblocks asserting a closed feedback loop that no code closes. Note the contrast with this run's own per-file lens output, which flagged `foldTokensPerPctObservation` and `foldOutputRatioObservation` as a duplicated EWMA blend to extract into one shared helper (.audit-tools/audit-findings.json:4423) — a local read sees two near-copies worth deduplicating and cannot see that one of the two has no production caller at all, so acting on that finding alone would refactor dead code into a shared helper. Whole-system pressure is what distinguishes the two, and this finding supersedes that one.

findings.title: The loop-until-dry adversary is the only review pass given neither the shared corpus nor its own prior findings — a 2,935-byte context-free prompt whose convergence terminator is exact-title equality, so it took 6 serial host rounds to do what the pipeline already holds the data to shortcut
findings.summary: Phase E is the pipeline's one genuinely ITERATIVE pass — N serial host_delegation pauses whose stated mandate is 'find what earlier rounds missed' — and it is the only pass whose per-round input contains neither the reviewed system nor the prior verdict. Measured on this run: the four persisted round prompts (.audit-tools/audit/steps/a-*/current-prompt.md) are each exactly 2,935 bytes and `diff` of round 3 against round 6 shows exactly TWO changed lines (the round ordinal and the prior COUNT); the whole payload is 8 aggregate rollup counts. The sibling passes in the SAME phase render 48,744-54,586 bytes of shared structural corpus (the six design-review prompts on disk). So each adversary round must re-derive a 1,397-component tree from scratch, and 5 completed rounds yielded 7/5/4/3/1 — 6 serial round trips for 20 findings. THE SUBSTRATE ALREADY EXISTS AND HAS TWO CONSUMERS: `DesignReviewSnapshot.prior_findings: Finding[]` (src/audit/orchestrator/designReviewSnapshot.ts:54, written at :128) is fed VERBATIM into the pass's prompt by the single-sourced `renderDiffReReviewSection` (src/shared/reReview/projectionDiff.ts:146-168, '### Your prior verdict (re-affirm it verbatim if the changes below do not affect it)'), which remediate's contract pipeline also consumes (src/remediate/contractPipeline/reviewSnapshot.ts:188). The challenge loop consumes none of it: `renderSecondOrderAdversaryPrompt` (src/audit/systemic/secondOrderAdversaryPrompt.ts:26-28) accepts `priorFindingCount: number`, and the call site takes that number off the array it would need to inject — `result.bundle.systemic_challenge?.findings.length ?? 0` (src/audit/cli/nextStepCommand.ts:1051). Cost of injecting it: id+lens+title for all 20 is 5,274 bytes (titles alone 4,091; full JSON 59,864) — under 10% of what ONE sibling prompt already spends. The access grant makes the omission exact rather than arguable: `access.read_paths` DOES include systemic_challenge.json (nextStepCommand.ts:1089), but `prompt: adversaryPrompt` (:1087) never names that path or mentions the register, so the prior set reaches the adversary only if the host notices the grant in current-step.json and folds it into the agent's briefing by hand — which is exactly what happened in this run, and is the recorded latent-failure signature the project's own auditor-agnostic-robustness rule bans ('only works because a capable host folded in guidance'). SECOND HALF, same root: convergence is decided by EXACT title equality. `foldChallengeRound` (src/audit/systemic/systemicChallengeLoop.ts:108-124) keys newness on `findingReEmissionKey`, which is `trim+lowercase(lens|category|title)` (src/shared/findings/dedupe.ts:300-306), and `converged` is set only by that `dry` bit — grep finds NO round cap anywhere. So a reworded restatement of a prior improvement registers as new, keeps the loop open, and costs another full serial adversary round; and the fuzzy collapse that would catch it lives in the very module the loop already imports from — `sameLensDedupe` (dedupe.ts:329: title word-Jaccard >=0.35/0.45 plus line-range or >=0.5 file-path overlap) — and ALREADY RUNS downstream in the same pipeline at src/audit/reporting/mergeFindings.ts:106, so the duplicate the loop paid a round trip for is silently collapsed at report time anyway. The context-free prompt also mis-prices the round to the quota gate: hostFanoutGate is handed `estInputBytes: Buffer.byteLength(adversaryPrompt)` = 2,935 (nextStepCommand.ts:1068) as the cost of a full-repo reconnaissance. Three changes, all reusing in-tree primitives: render the prior register into the round prompt through the existing re-review section rather than passing a scalar count; give the round the same `renderSharedStructuralContext` corpus its sibling passes get (which, with the prefix reordering, is then cache-eligible ACROSS rounds, not just across the fan-out); and decide newness with the fuzzy identity `sameLensDedupe` already implements, plus a round cap, so convergence cannot be deferred indefinitely by rewording. DISTINCT from the two nearest prior items: the fan-out-caching item concerns prefix ORDER inside prompts that DO carry the corpus and asserts in passing that the challenge rounds 're-render it again per round' — measurement above refutes that, they render NO corpus at all; and the PRIORITY-serialization item concerns two independent passes that could run concurrently, whereas these rounds are genuinely sequential and the finding is that their per-round input is empty, which is what makes the sequence long.

findings.title: The nightly ledger factored its core and duplicated its two shells, so the fix for the settled-vs-answered incident landed in the CLI half only and the browser review surface still cannot record the disposition that fix introduced
findings.summary: scripts/nightly did the hard half right and the easy half twice. items.mjs is a genuinely shared core (one open-items store, one subject_key scheme, one partitionBySettled, one evaluateProbes - which scripts/shared/triage-backlog.mjs correctly IMPORTS rather than reimplements), but the two entry points onto it are forks. (a) Guards: serve.mjs's POST /answer handler carries the comment 'Same guards as answer.mjs' (:168) and then implements them independently - and they have already diverged. answer.mjs:160 is `wontfixAt !== -1 ? 'wontfix' : questionAt !== -1 ? 'question' : 'settled'`; serve.mjs:192 is `disposition === 'wontfix' ? 'wontfix' : 'settled'`, and its client half (:77) only ever emits settled or wontfix, so there is no `question` control at all. `question` is not cosmetic: answer.mjs:153-158 records why it exists - 'Two of the eighteen determinations on 2026-07-28 were exactly this shape and were filed as settled, which made them unaskable while carrying no answer anyone could act on'. The browser UI is the surface an operator actually reaches (render-digest.mjs:308 spawns serve.mjs whenever items are open), and it silently coerces every non-wontfix answer to settled - reproducing the exact failure the CLI fix was written to prevent, in the half the fix never reached. (b) Renderers: the item core is shared but each shell keeps its own per-item renderer (render-digest.mjs:172 renderStaticItem vs serve.mjs:26 renderInteractiveItem) plus its own root-flag/open-browser CLI block. (c) Redundant reads: one POST /answer cycle calls partitionBySettled four times (serve.mjs:116, :173, :199, plus :220 at startup), each re-reading both JSON files and re-running evaluateProbes' file reads. (d) The whole ledger sits outside every durability guarantee src/ provides for this exact shape: items.mjs writeJson (:65-67) is a bare writeFileSync with no lock and no temp-then-rename, while two writers can race it (the HTTP server at serve.mjs:192 and the CLI at answer.mjs:174, plus the SessionStart hook writing last-viewed.json) - and src/ already owns withFileLock, createLockedJsonStore and atomic writeJsonFile, used for the structurally identical friction and remediation-state ledgers. scripts/ is reached by no tsconfig, so nothing typechecks any of it. The fix is the project's own default: one guard+disposition module and one renderer consumed by both shells, and route the ledger writes through the shared locked/atomic store rather than a fourth hand-rolled one.

findings.title: The one provider that writes model-returned files itself never receives the node's declared write scope, and its containment check is lexical so an in-worktree symlink escapes
findings.summary:
TRUST BOUNDARY: `openai-compatible` is architecturally different from the agentic providers — it POSTs a packet to a `/chat/completions` endpoint and then APPLIES the returned `{files, result}` into the node's worktree itself, so the tool (not an agent's Edit tool) performs the writes. That makes its apply loop a first-class write boundary for untrusted model output.

WHAT IT CHECKS: root containment plus a control-plane exclusion. Each returned `file.path` goes through `safeResolveInRepo` → `resolveWithinRoot(repoRoot, candidate, { allowRoot: false })` (src/shared/providers/openAiCompatibleProvider.ts:470, :911-915), and a path under the `.audit-tools` control-plane dir is skipped. A non-contained path fails the whole launch.

TWO GAPS: (1) It never checks the node's declared `write_paths` — verified by grepping the provider: `write_paths` does not appear in the file at all, and the provider's own comment concedes the point ("The worktree branch diff is still the write-scope ground truth at merge; here we defend against a path escaping the worktree entirely", :453-455). So write scope for this provider is deferred entirely to accept-time adjudication — which DR-006 shows does not confine to declared scope on a single-block wave, and DR-007 shows is inert on the main-tree dispatch paths. Deferring to a downstream gate is sound only when that gate holds; here neither condition is guaranteed. (2) `resolveWithinRoot` is purely lexical — it calls `resolve()`/`relative()` and never `realpath` (src/shared/io/pathContainment.ts:43-58). A tracked symlink inside the worktree pointing outside it therefore resolves as contained, the write lands outside the tree, and because the symlink blob itself is unchanged the write produces no `git diff` entry — so it is invisible to the branch-diff ground truth as well as to the containment check.

RECOMMENDED CHANGE: pass the node's declared `write_paths` into `LaunchFreshSessionInput` and reject a returned file outside them at apply time, so the provider that performs the write is the one that enforces the scope (fail-closed at the boundary rather than relying on a downstream gate with known holes). For the symlink half, resolve the final path with `realpath` on the existing parent directory before writing and re-run containment on the resolved result; `canonicalizeFilePath` already has a `resolveSymlinks` option, so this is a matter of threading it through rather than new machinery.

findings.title: The remediate smoke pair is a hand-rolled fork of the audit smoke pair - no shared flow module, duplicated harness and npm-env scrub, and six CLI spawns to assert six fields of one JSON
findings.summary: The audit side single-sources its smoke behaviour: both audit smokes import phases from scripts/audit/smoke-audit-flow.mjs and process helpers from scripts/shared/smoke-process.mjs (createRunCommand, createSmokeLog, platformCommand), and assert with node:assert/strict. The remediate side shares none of it - grep for smoke-audit-flow / smoke-process across scripts/remediate returns zero hits. Instead smoke-linked-remediate-code.mjs (148 lines) and smoke-packaged-remediate-code.mjs (182 lines) are two standalone scripts that each re-implement their own check(label, fn) pass/fail harness, their own spawn wrapper over child_process.spawnSync, and - in the packaged one - an isolatedNpmEnv() that duplicates createIsolatedNpmEnv() in smoke-packaged-audit-code.mjs almost statement for statement (same npm_config_* strip, same node_auth_token/npm_token strip, same forced npm_config_dry_run=false). The fork has two measurable consequences. (a) Coverage asymmetry: smoke:packaged-remediate-code runs in 2,117 ms against smoke:packaged-audit-code's 210,611 ms because it never drives a remediate flow at all - it asserts install, --version twice, and two postinstall file properties, so a name that promises packaged-install parity delivers bootstrap-only. (b) Waste: smoke-linked-remediate-code.mjs calls run('next-step', ...) six separate times, spawning the CLI once per assertion to re-derive and re-serialize the same JSON, where one spawn plus one parse would serve all six field assertions. This is precisely the 'one core, two draws' case the project states as its default - the smoke harness is one shared core with a per-mode flow module and a per-mode installation-shape adapter, not two forks - and extracting it is the fix the repo's own 'extract shared logic, do not drift-test it' rule prescribes.

findings.title: The safety net costs 45-51 minutes and 7,860 tests, and is noisy enough to need a second mechanism to interpret
findings.summary: The test tree is larger than the product it guards, and slow and flaky enough that its signal must be post-processed to be usable. Measured from .audit-tools-profile/vitest-history.ndjson: full-suite runs are 565 files and 7,860 tests at 2,730-3,070 seconds of summed wall time, with a maximum recorded 9,510s. By line count the tests (~179,300 lines across tests/audit, tests/remediate, tests/shared) exceed the source (~143,700 lines across src/, scripts/, wrapper/, dispatch/). Six consecutive full runs on 2026-07-29 reported failure counts of 1, 0, 5, 0, 0, 0 — the same tree, different verdicts. That noise floor forced a second apparatus into existence purely to interpret the first: scripts/shared/test-flake-baseline.json, scripts/shared/rebaseline-flakes.mjs, and tests/shared/parallel-flake-baseline.test.ts. The rebaseline script's own header records why writing it had to become a manual act — the baseline used to be written by every run, and the last one recorded two genuine regressions, one as parallel_flaky, the status that actively explains a red away. A gate that can launder a regression into a known flake is worse than a smaller gate, and the repo's own audit reached the same conclusion independently (theme T-007, the test suite can pass without testing). There is also a declared coverage hole: tsconfig.test.json sets checkJs:false, so .mjs test files are not typechecked (see DR-020 for the same hole across the enforcement layer). Recommendation: split the suite explicitly by cost, running a fast deterministic core on every commit and quarantining the slow orchestration files (tests/audit/audit-code-completion.test.ts alone is recorded at a 285-470s file wall) into a separate scheduled job. A gate whose verdict needs a baseline to decode is not yet a gate; the goal should be deleting the flake-baseline mechanism, not maintaining it.

findings.title: The steal-claim crash-recovery path (orphaned .steal sidecar reclamation) has zero test coverage
findings.summary: fileLock's stale-steal protocol is crash-tolerant only because a steal claim older than STALE_LOCK_MS is treated as abandoned and reclaimed — the branch that prevents a permanently wedged lock (and with it, all quota-state and credential writes) after a stealer dies mid-steal. No test anywhere in the tree references the `.steal` sidecar or STEAL_CLAIM_SUFFIX: the otherwise-thorough fileLock suites (fileLock.test.ts's 20 cases including the concurrent-steal mutual-exclusion property, fileLock-clock-seam.test.ts) never orphan a claim file, so both the reclaim branch (stale claim removed, acquisition proceeds) and the leave-alone branch (fresh in-progress claim respected) are exercised by no test. A regression here — e.g. inverting the age comparison — would wedge every lock behind a crashed stealer and no suite would go red.
evidence: src/shared/quota/fileLock.ts:84-88,95-108 - the crash-tolerance contract ('a claim older than STALE_LOCK_MS is treated as abandoned and reclaimed ... so the lock can never wedge permanently') lives entirely in this branch.

findings.title: The test tree's three-way directory taxonomy is not a partition: shared modules are tested from all three directories in duplicate, and the meta-guards' reach is accidental rather than declared
findings.summary: tests/{audit,remediate,shared} mirrors the three source areas, but the mapping is not a function: 25 test files under tests/audit and tests/remediate have no local src/ import at all and test shared modules exclusively. The result is independent, partial, non-identical coverings of the same code. audit-tools/shared/quota/fileLock is tested by four files across three directories — tests/shared/fileLock.test.ts (676 lines), fileLock-clock-seam.test.ts (66), tests/audit/quota-file-lock.test.ts (94), tests/remediate/quota-file-lock.test.ts (204) — where the last two overlap but are not equal (only the remediate copy exercises stale-lock reaping), so neither is authoritative and a behaviour change requires finding all four. runSlidingWindow has three, in different assertion styles; the error parsers and quota sources are likewise doubled. The same accident afflicts the meta-test layer: three tests-invariants files (1,276 lines) assert properties of the test corpus, each scoped to its own directory by construction (tests/remediate/remediate-tests-invariants.test.ts:22 sets TESTS_DIR to __dirname, tests/shared/shared-tests-invariants.test.mjs:15 likewise, tests/audit/audit-tests-invariants.test.ts:18 scopes to tests/audit for most assertions), so 'no test file has a bare it() at column 0' holds only over tests/remediate and 'no .test.mjs imports node:test/jest/mocha' only over tests/shared. The reach of each guard is a side effect of which sprint wrote it, not a decision — and credit where due, the two genuinely corpus-wide properties (the dist/-import bans) were correctly generalized to ALL_TEST_DIRS, which shows the generalization is cheap. The project's guard-reach registry is the right mechanism and already declares one of these gaps (scripts/guard-reach-data.mjs notes the vi.spyOn barrel guard scans only tests/remediate), but it declares only that one, so the tests/** row understates the real uncovered set. A related decay: many assertions in these files are not invariants but pinned historical facts — a named test file does not define a local helper, another imports a symbol from a specific module, an either-or assertion count does not grow beyond known debt — i.e. universally-quantified properties degenerated into a list of remembered incidents, the same current-state-not-durable-concept decay the documentation philosophy bans, except tests are outside that ban's reach. Recommendation: partition the test tree by the module under test rather than by the orchestrator that happens to call it (shared-module tests live only under tests/shared, merged rather than tripled); state each meta-guard's scanned set as data over tests/** with explicit exclusions, in the same registry that already models this for hooks; and hold meta-assertions to the invariant bar, moving per-file pins into the test they concern.

findings.title: The two-tier dependency policy was applied to TOML and YAML and then stopped: XML is parsed with regex, JSONC with a hand-written state machine, and globs with a hand-rolled translator
findings.summary: The project wrote down exactly the right rule — a format whose grammar we do not own is correctness-sensitive, so import a vetted pure-JS parser and wrap it so malformed input degrades to empty — and then applied it to two formats. src/audit/extractors/graphManifestEdges/toml.ts and yaml.ts use smol-toml and yaml, and both carry docstrings recording that they REPLACED a hand-rolled line scanner which dropped dotted-key and inline-table forms, so the policy is documented with its own bug history. The remaining formats in the same directory never got the treatment: maven.ts (99 lines) parses pom.xml with stripXmlComments, five hardcoded XML entities in decodeXmlText, and nested modules regexes — so CDATA, namespaces, any other entity, and attribute-bearing forms are mishandled and a multi-module Maven repo silently loses workspace edges; jsonc.ts (113 lines) hand-writes a character-by-character comment stripper and trailing-comma remover before JSON.parse, where jsonc-parser (pure JS, the implementation VS Code itself uses for tsconfig) exists; workspace.ts:62-79 hand-translates glob patterns into RegExp where picomatch is the pure-JS standard; go.ts (202 lines) hand-scans go.work directives; packageJson.ts:17-18 extracts script cross-references with a regex. Each is the same bet — that a regex over a grammar we do not own will not silently drop an edge — and each lost edge propagates into the risk register, the unit clustering and the review packets, so the failure is invisible and downstream. Recommendation: finish the policy in one pass — fast-xml-parser for pom.xml, jsonc-parser for JSONC/tsconfig, picomatch for glob matching (also the fix for DR-032) — all pure JS with no native build, all wrapped to degrade to empty on malformed input, exactly as toml.ts and yaml.ts already are.

findings.title: The worker result contract has two independent implementations - the strict zod schema published to workers and a 1,141-line hand-written gate that admits them - and they demonstrably disagree
findings.summary: One contract, two implementations, no cross-check. (a) The contract a worker is TOLD to satisfy is generated from zod: WorkerAuditResultSchema (workerSchemas.ts:86) and WorkerAuditResultsSchema (:107) render schemas/audit_result.schema.json and audit_results.schema.json through WORKER_SCHEMA_SOURCES (:113-128) / renderWorkerJsonSchema (:139), and those files are strict - `.strict()` on every object, enum-constrained lens/severity/confidence, min(1) on file_coverage, affected_files and evidence. (b) The contract that actually decides admission is src/audit/validation/auditResults.ts - 1,141 lines, 26 functions, exactly ONE occurrence of the string 'Schema' in the whole file and it is inside a comment. It is the sole gate on inbound results, at 7 production call sites (auditStep.ts:349, mergeAndIngestCommand.ts:540, submitPacketCommand.ts:111, validateResultCommand.ts:77, validateResultsCommand.ts:19, workerRunCommand.ts:70, workerResult.ts:32), and its shape tier re-derives imperatively what the zod schema already states declaratively: validateRequiredStringField (:153), validateFindingRequiredFields (:204), validateFindingEnums (:222 - 41 lines to check that severity/confidence/lens are in three Sets the zod enums already define), validateAffectedFiles (:263), validateEvidence (:336), validateOptionalStringArray (:411), validateFileCoverageEntry (:763). Nothing anywhere validates an inbound submission against WorkerAuditResultsSchema, and no test compares the two. I demonstrated the divergence empirically: a result carrying two unrecognized keys is REJECTED by WorkerAuditResultsSchema.safeParse (`unrecognized_keys`) and ACCEPTED by validateAuditResults with zero issues - so the published contract forbids what the gate admits, which is the concrete form of the recorded 'the validator ignores unknown keys' hazard and means a renamed or typo'd field lands silently. The repo already believes this is not the case: tests/audit/schema-contracts.test.ts:33-38 states as its premise that 'every artifact contract is single-sourced as a zod schema ... there is no separate JSON-schema document or hand-rolled validator any more'. The better arrangement is the split workerSchemas.ts:96-99 already articulates for one field but never generalized: WorkerAuditResultsSchema.safeParse IS the shape tier (it is already the published contract and already in-process at ingest), and auditResults.ts keeps only what a flat schema genuinely cannot express - identity equality against the ASSIGNED task (validateResultIdentityFields :690), file_coverage[].total_lines against real on-disk line counts (validateResultFileCoverage :856, isSignificantLineCountDivergence :38), coversAffectedSpan (:658), and the conditional reviewed_clean rule (validateResultFindings :891). Distinct from the two adjacent recorded items: DR-024 is duplication whose answer is a parity test, and here there is no parity test at all; DR-043 concerns the zod-to-json-schema DEPENDENCY, not which implementation adjudicates the contract.

findings.title: The wrapper layer is a second audit/remediate fork nobody has extracted: 3,568 of 4,126 lines live in five near-identical file pairs whose real delta is 282 lines, and only the audit half is tested
findings.summary: wrapper/ ships 12 .mjs files totalling 4,126 lines, and five of them are pairwise forks: install-hosts (1,189 / 1,183 lines), opencode (281 / 249), io (155 / 145), legacy (125 / 125), install-renderers (58 / 58) — 1,808 audit-side + 1,760 remediate-side = 3,568 lines, 86% of the whole layer. Measured divergence after normalizing only the tool name (s/audit-code/TOOL/, s/remediate-code/TOOL/): 120 + 106 + 10 + 36 + 10 = 282 differing lines. Inspecting the install-hosts diff, essentially all of it is the slash-command name, one label ('audit workflow' vs 'remediation workflow'), the permission-assert helper name, and comment rewrapping — the two files carry the SAME descriptor-driven engine over the SAME four host definitions (INSTALL_HOST_DEFINITIONS for codex / opencode / vscode / antigravity, INSTALL_HOST_ORDER, INSTALL_PROFILE_FLAGS, buildInstallDirective, the per-host async verify closures). The internal design is already the right one — data-driven host descriptors, renderers derived from the ONE canonical loader body — which is exactly why the duplication is unnecessary: what differs is a tool descriptor, not an algorithm. This is the project's stated default (one shared core + per-mode policy, extract rather than drift-test) unapplied to its own install surface, and unlike the provider forks there is not even a parity test holding the two halves together. The verification is correspondingly lopsided: the audit half has ~2,362 lines of behavioural tests (tests/audit/audit-code-wrapper.test.ts 1,980, host-asset-renderer-drift.test.ts 229, a7.test.ts 153), while the remediate half appears in exactly one test — tests/shared/audit-tools-path-guard.test.ts — and only as a path literal in a scanner allowlist, so 1,760 lines of shipped install logic have no behavioural coverage at all. One host-install engine parameterized by {toolName, slashCommand, installDir, permissionAssert} plus two thin adapters collapses ~1,700 lines and makes the existing audit-side test suite bind BOTH bins.

findings.title: Two divergent definitions of "in declared write scope" run inside the same accept: exact equality vs prefix/glob containment
findings.summary:
INFERRED CONTRACT: "in the declared write scope" is one predicate. The repo treats duplicated guards as correctness work, not style — `pathContainment.ts` was created precisely because a containment check existed in five hand-rolled copies and one was subtly wrong, and project memory records "five copies of a guard hid two bugs" and "a 'lockstep' comment is the duplication tell — extract, don't drift-test".

COUNTEREXAMPLE: two different predicates decide it within a single node accept. `writeScopeViolations` uses EXACT string membership — `declared.has(rel)` after `toRepoRelative` (src/remediate/steps/dispatch/common.ts:286-290) — so a declared directory does not cover a file inside it. `isUnderWritePaths`, used by the commit's force-add pass for gitignored new files, uses PREFIX plus glob containment — `target === literalPrefix || target.startsWith(`${literalPrefix}/`)`, plus leading-wildcard handling (src/remediate/steps/dispatch/worktreeLifecycle.ts:765-787). Consequence for a block declaring `src/foo`: a worker-created `src/foo/new.ts` is IN scope for the commit force-add and OUT of scope for the write-scope gate. Today that divergence is masked by the unowned-grant of DR-006, which is what makes it a latent gap rather than a live break — remove or tighten that grant (as DR-006 recommends) and the two predicates start disagreeing visibly.

SECONDARY DIVERGENCE in the same area: `toRepoRelative` (common.ts:24-31) normalizes backslashes and strips an absolute in-root prefix, but does not strip a leading `./`, does not case-fold, and never calls `resolve`/`realpath`. Its sibling normalizer in shared, `normalizeRepoPath` (src/shared/validation/findingGrounding.ts:46-48), DOES strip `./` and case-fold. So a declared `./src/a.ts` or a mis-cased `Src/A.ts` fails to match git's `src/a.ts` on a case-insensitive filesystem — again currently absorbed by the unowned-grant.

RECOMMENDED CHANGE: extract one scope-membership predicate (declared-path list + candidate → boolean, with the glob/prefix semantics decided once) into shared and have both `writeScopeViolations` and the force-add pass call it, per the project's stated preference for extraction over drift tests. Fold the `./` strip and case-folding decision into that one normalizer so declared and actual paths are compared in a single canonical form.

findings.title: Vitest's unit of parallelism is the FILE, so the suite is floored at its largest single file (268.7 s) no matter how it is sharded — and the in-file lever is untouched: 1.0% of tests are concurrent and maxConcurrency is left at the default 5
findings.summary: Every improvement proposed for suite latency so far operates ACROSS files (shard count, duration-balanced shard assignment, build reuse). That lever saturates against a wall nobody priced, because `vitest --shard` partitions the file list and never splits a file: the achievable wall for ANY shard count is bounded below by max(single-file duration). Measured from the repo's own most recent full-suite ledger record (.audit-tools-profile/vitest-history.ndjson, 2026-07-29T16:49:18Z, 565 files, wallSummed 2,730,730 ms = 45.5 min, run 2,368,424 ms = 86.7%, collect 303,386 ms = 11.1%): the four heaviest files are tests/audit/audit-code-completion.test.ts 268,736 ms, tests/audit/audit-code-wrapper.test.ts 220,511 ms, tests/audit/next-step.test.ts 184,607 ms and tests/audit/linux-cycle-regression.test.ts 145,291 ms — 819,145 ms, exactly 30.0% of the whole suite, with the top ten at 44.8%. Ideal 4-way balance is 682,683 ms per shard, so at four shards the largest file is not yet binding; but the remedy of 'raise the shard count for finer granularity' hits a hard floor at 268.7 s and buys nothing past roughly ten shards. The in-file lever, which is the one that can go below that floor, is almost entirely unused, and the repo has already proved it safe. (a) Adoption is 78 `.concurrent` blocks out of 7,844 total test blocks — 1.0%. The largest file, audit-code-completion.test.ts, is FOUR tests (lines 340, 391, 467, 520) with zero `.concurrent`, i.e. ~67 s per test strictly serial — while its sibling audit-code-wrapper.test.ts runs 42 of its 43 tests as `it.concurrent`, over the same kind of CLI round-trip, so the pattern is established, reviewed and green. Both files already create per-test temp dirs via `mkdtemp`, which is the isolation that makes in-file concurrency safe; the sequential one is not sequential for a stated reason, it simply never adopted the sibling's pattern. (b) Even the files that DID adopt it are capped: vitest 3.2.6's `maxConcurrency` default is 5 (node_modules/vitest/dist/chunks/defaults.B7q_naMc.js:104) and vitest.config.ts sets none of maxConcurrency / fileParallelism / maxWorkers / isolate / pool — grep for maxConcurrency across the tracked tree returns zero hits — so audit-code-wrapper.test.ts's 42 concurrent tests execute as nine sequential waves of five, on tests that are dominated by waiting on child processes rather than CPU. (c) linux-cycle-regression.test.ts is 145.3 s in a SINGLE test, so it is atomic to every scheduling mechanism the runner has: no shard count, no worker count and no concurrency setting can reduce it, only splitting the scenario. Three mechanical changes, in increasing order of effort: set `maxConcurrency` in vitest.config.ts to the real safe ceiling for IO-bound round-trip tests (the config is already the single home for suite policy, next to the deliberate isolate/setupFiles comments); convert the heavy sequential files to the `it.concurrent` form their sibling already uses; and split the one-test file. This matters beyond the 45-minute number because the same distribution sets the CI critical path and the release gate: a 30%-of-suite concentration in four files means the safety net's latency is decided by four authoring choices rather than by the runner's configuration, and the runner's configuration is where the project's own rules say a property like this belongs. Distinct from the earlier cross-file finding (build reuse plus duration-balanced sharding), whose stated target of ~121 s is unreachable for exactly the reason above, and distinct from the conceptual 'safety net costs 45-51 minutes and 7,860 tests' finding, which prices the net's total size and noise rather than the runner's parallelism unit.

findings.title: weightedGraph pair key uses a space separator, corrupting edges for file paths containing spaces
findings.summary: buildStructureSources' weightedGraph aggregates undirected coupling edges under the key `${lo} ${hi}` and later splits it at the FIRST space via key.indexOf(" "). A repo path containing a space (legal on every OS) makes the split land inside the first path, producing garbage endpoints (e.g. a='my', b='dir/file.ts my dir/file.ts') that are not in the node universe — the real coupling edge is silently lost or mis-attributed for every space-containing file, skewing every behavior partition built from these graphs. The sibling dedup in normalizeExternal.ts uses a NUL ('\0') separator for exactly this reason.

src/audit/decompose/sources.ts:48-49 - key.indexOf(" ") finds the first space, which for a space-containing `lo` path sits inside the path; key.slice(0, idx)/key.slice(idx+1) then yield endpoints that are not real files.
src/audit/adapters/normalizeExternal.ts:118 - the same pattern done safely elsewhere in this packet: deduped.set(`${from}\0${to}\0${kind ?? ""}`, edge) uses NUL, which cannot appear in a path.

findings.title: (judge-added) There is no unattended mode and no budget on operator pauses, while the stated destination is a scheduled autonomous loop
findings.summary: Two perspectives noted individual interactive gates as friction (DR-017, DR-018); none noticed that the gates are accumulating against a roadmap that requires their absence. CLAUDE.md:247 states the standing plan: redesign before scheduled autonomy — architecture stabilizes first, then build a scheduled audit-remediate-PR loop on the new architecture. Nothing in the current design moves toward that. Verified: src/audit/cli/args.ts declares no unattended, non-interactive, headless or assume-yes flag of any kind, so there is no mode in which the operator-facing gates are skipped or pre-answered; src/audit/orchestrator/executors.ts declares 13 host_delegation executors (of ~25 obligations), and src/audit/orchestrator/hostInputPause.ts exists specifically to single-source WHERE the drain stops for the operator, so the pause set is a first-class concept with no ceiling attached to it. Every lap that adds a gate adds another point at which a scheduled run would halt, and there is no counter, budget, or test asserting how many operator pauses a default run contains — while the project meticulously budgets packet counts, scope files, drain steps and backlog entry lengths. Two consequences. First, the stabilize-then-automate sequencing has no exit condition: nothing distinguishes 'architecture is stable enough to automate' from 'architecture has more gates than last month'. Second, the pause count is the actual blocking constraint on the capstone, and it is invisible in planning, so work that adds a gate is never priced against the roadmap it delays. Recommendation, cheap and mostly mechanical: derive the operator-pause set from the existing data (executors.ts kind plus hostInputPause.ts) and report it as a number in the same profile history the project already keeps for verify:checks and vitest, so the trend is visible; then decide the pause budget for a default run and treat exceeding it as a design question rather than a detail. Separately, decide deliberately whether an unattended mode is the eventual shape — if it is, each new gate needs a declared non-interactive answer at the time it is added, which is far cheaper than retrofitting answers for 13 of them later.

findings.title: A failed credential persist after a successful refresh grant silently discards the rotated tokens and can brick the stored refresh token
findings.summary: refreshAndPersist runs the refresh grant (which rotates the token pair server-side) and then persists via writeCredentialsAtomic. If the persist throws — on Windows, renameSync over a credentials file concurrently held open by the Claude CLI commonly fails EPERM/EBUSY — the outer catch swallows everything and returns null: the freshly granted access token is discarded instead of being used in-memory, and the on-disk refresh token has already been invalidated by the rotation, so every future refresh fails until the operator re-logs-in. The code's own double-check comment acknowledges that losing a rotation 'would invalidate the first refresh token and brick the credential', but only guards the concurrent-probe path, not the persist-failure path.
evidence: src/shared/quota/claudeOAuthQuotaSource.ts:241 - runRefreshGrant consumes the stored refresh token before any persistence attempt; grant success + persist failure leaves disk state pointing at a consumed token.

src/shared/quota/claudeOAuthQuotaSource.ts:258 - the catch collapses lock timeout, grant failure, and persist failure into one silent null; grant.access_token obtained just before is not returned or retried.

src/shared/quota/claudeOAuthQuotaSource.ts:36 (module doc) - the double-checked lock exists precisely because a lost rotation 'would invalidate the first refresh token and brick the credential', yet the write-failure leg of the same hazard is unhandled.
Project context: transient EPERM/EBUSY on rename under concurrent readers is a known Windows failure mode in this codebase (documented test-failure protocol treats EPERM as an expected flake class).

findings.title: Finding identity anchor is affected_files[0], but merge passes SORT affected_files — a merged-in file that sorts before the primary silently moves the identity signature
findings.summary: findingIdentityFields derives the tier-1 structural anchor from finding.affected_files[0], and the module documents that identity 'stays put as additional re-emitted files are unioned into it across passes and runs'. But the merge passes that grow the union (upsertFindingByIdentity, sameLensDedupe, audit's crossLensDedupe draw) call mergeAffectedFiles with sort=true, which re-sorts affected_files by path — so when a re-emission contributes a file that sorts lexicographically before the original primary, affected_files[0] (and therefore findingIdentityKey, the stable-id hash input, and primaryPath grouping) changes. Whether a finding merged also determines whether its files were ever sorted, so the same logical finding can carry different identities across passes/runs, churning stable ids, theme references, and the coverage-ledger key the signature exists to hold still.
evidence: src/shared/findingIdentitySignature.ts:128 - the tier-1 anchor is whatever file happens to be at index 0 of affected_files; the docstring (lines 89-93) claims the signature is independent of the merged file list.

src/shared/findings/dedupe.ts:68-71 - mergeAffectedFiles(sort=true) re-orders affected_files by path; upsertFindingByIdentity (line 402) and sameLensDedupe (line 361) always pass sort=true, so after any merge affected_files[0] becomes the lexicographically-first path — a union that adds a path sorting before the primary changes the anchor and hence the identity key.
src/shared/findings/dedupe.ts:381-386 - a finding that never merges keeps its worker-emitted (unsorted) file order, so identity additionally depends on merge history, not only on content.

findings.title: Host-session near-wall band never decays: one recorded limit throttles the pool to 5% for the process lifetime
findings.summary: HostSessionQuotaSource.probeUsage reports the near-wall band (remaining_pct 0.05) whenever the window is open but `this.tracker != null`. The tracker is set on any recorded limit and is only ever cleared on escalation — there is no success path, decay, or API to reset it, and the elapsed-reset check exists only inside recordLimit. So after a single transient session limit, the source keeps answering 0.05 for its key for the rest of the process; because it is prepended in the composite cascade and the first snapshot wins, it permanently masks the proactive source's true (recovered) reading and holds the pool in the CRITICAL throttle band even long after the account has fully recovered. The source's own comment scopes the band to 'this window cycle', which the implementation does not enforce.
evidence: src/shared/quota/hostSessionQuotaSource.ts:323-328 - probeUsage answers near-wall (0.05) whenever tracker is non-null and the window is open; there is no check that the tracker's last_reset_ms has elapsed.

src/shared/quota/hostSessionQuotaSource.ts:255-260,284-285 - the tracker is (re)armed on every recorded limit and nulled ONLY inside the escalation branch; no public method or success path ever clears it, so it survives for the object's lifetime.

src/shared/quota/hostSessionQuotaSource.ts:59-64 - the WINDOW_NEAR_WALL_REMAINING_PCT doc scopes the band to 'a limit has been seen this window cycle ... and a fresh same-cycle limit is being tracked', which probeUsage does not implement.

src/shared/quota/compositeQuotaSource.ts:120-125 + src/shared/quota/hostPool.ts:183-189 - the host-session source is deliberately prepended and first-snapshot-wins, so its stale 0.05 snapshot shadows the claude-oauth proactive source's real reading for the host pool key.

findings.title: Line-count failure sentinel 0 propagates as an authoritative expected line count
findings.summary: buildLineIndex/buildLineIndexForPaths convert every per-file counting failure (transient EMFILE/EACCES/EBUSY as well as file-not-found) into an index entry of 0 that is indistinguishable from a genuinely empty file; only stderr distinguishes the cases, the returned data does not. validate-results feeds that index into validateAuditResults, where the 0 is treated as the authoritative disk line count and isSignificantLineCountDivergence(got, 0) makes any honest declared total_lines past the absolute floor a hard-reject CE-009 error, so a transient IO failure turns valid worker results into validation errors and exitCode 1; addFileLineCountHints likewise emits misleading file_line_counts of 0 for such files.
evidence: src/audit/cli/lineIndex.ts:37 - every counting failure returns [file.path, 0], so the returned index encodes 'count failed' as 'zero lines'; the COR-c868f53d comment fixed only the stderr message wording, not the returned data.

src/audit/cli/validateResultsCommand.ts:16 - the failure-defaulted index is passed as options.lineIndex into validateAuditResults with no accompanying failure mask, so the consumer cannot tell a failed count from an empty file.

src/audit/validation/auditResults.ts:819-834 - expectedLineCount = normLineIndex.get(entryNorm) treats the 0 sentinel as the actual disk count; per the CE-009 gate, an expected of 0 makes any delta past the absolute floor (2) a significant divergence and hard-reject, so a transient IO failure (the fd-exhaustion class LINE_COUNT_BATCH_SIZE exists to mitigate) falsely rejects honest results.
src/audit/cli/lineIndex.ts:93-97 - addFileLineCountHints copies the same 0 sentinel into task.file_line_counts, presenting failed-to-count files to workers as 0-line files.

findings.summary: mergeWorktree resolves `git rev-parse <branch>` (the tip) and cherry-picks that single commit. findings.title: Model-scoped usage limits matched on display_name before id, so a non-matching display name hides the model's own quota window
findings.summary: scopedModelName returns the FIRST non-blank of [display_name, id] and limitAppliesToModel then substring-matches that one value against the provider/model key. When a limits[] entry carries both a human display name (e.g. "Claude Opus 4.5", with spaces/capitalization) and a machine id (e.g. "claude-opus-5"), the display name wins, fails the substring test against a hyphenated model key, and the entry is EXCLUDED from both pickBindingWindow and collectWindows — even though matching on the id would have succeeded. The model's own (often most-constraining) window is silently dropped, so remaining_pct over-reports headroom and the scheduler dispatches into the wall.
findings.impact: Over-optimistic quota snapshots for exactly the model being dispatched; the fix direction is to try BOTH identifiers (match if either substring-hits) rather than first-non-blank-wins.

src/shared/quota/claudeOAuthQuotaSource.ts:427-441 - pickBindingWindow drops non-matching model-scoped entries from the binding computation, so the miss directly inflates remaining_pct.

findings.title: No 'error' handler on child stdin: a worker that exits before draining stdinText can crash the whole process with an unhandled EPIPE
findings.summary: spawnLoggedCommand pipes the prompt via spawnedChild.stdin.end(this.input.stdinText) but never attaches an 'error' listener to the stdin stream. If the child exits before consuming the (often large) prompt — bad flag, immediate refusal, instant crash — the write fails with EPIPE (or ECONNRESET/EOF on Windows), which Node emits as an 'error' event on the stdin socket; with no listener that becomes an uncaughtException that takes down the orchestrator process instead of settling this one launch as rejected.
evidence: src/shared/providers/spawnLoggedCommand.ts:336 - stdin.end(text) is the only interaction with the stdin stream; handlers are wired for the child ('error', 'exit', 'close') and for stdout/stderr data, but not for stdin's own 'error' event.
The child-level 'error' listener (line 360) does not receive stream-level write failures; Node routes EPIPE on the stdin pipe to the stream's 'error' event, which is fatal when unhandled.

Every stdin-delivering provider (claude-worker, codex, opencode, claude-code) funnels through this one spawn substrate, so the blast radius is any dispatch wave whose worker dies before reading its prompt.

findings.title: No tracing standard for a system whose hardest debugging problem is multi-provider parallel dispatch; observability is a bespoke JSONL log plus a private profiling stack
findings.summary: The product's distinctive behaviour is fanning bounded work units out across many providers, models and worktrees concurrently, under quota pacing, with retries, quarantine and re-dispatch. Understanding what happened in such a run — which node went to which backend, what it cost, where the wall-clock went, why a lane stalled — is the central operational question, and the answer is currently assembled from purpose-built parts: src/shared/observability/runLog.ts (84 lines, append-only JSONL with a fixed event-kind union and a correlationId field), src/shared/io/tokenUsageLedger.ts, src/audit/systemic/aggregateMetricsDigest.ts, scripts/shared/profile.mjs, a 492-line custom vitest timing reporter, and scripts/nightly/render-digest.mjs rendering an HTML digest. correlationId is, in effect, a hand-rolled trace context. OpenTelemetry now covers this exact shape: spans with parent/child causality replace correlation-id joins, and the GenAI semantic conventions standardize model, token-usage and cost attributes — precisely what the token ledger and cost-ranking layers already track privately. Because OTLP is a wire format with a file exporter, adopting it does not require infrastructure: a run can emit a trace file any mature trace viewer reads, which would replace the bespoke digest renderer and profiling scripts with tooling the project does not maintain — the same consume-a-table-maintained-by-someone-else logic already applied to model metadata. Confidence is medium because there is a real tension worth weighing: the project is a zero-infrastructure npm package and an SDK plus exporters is a non-trivial dependency footprint, so the honest options are the full OTel SDK, a thin hand-written OTLP-JSON emitter conforming to the standard schema (keeping the current 84-line logger's footprint while gaining the ecosystem), or a deliberate decision to stay bespoke. Recommendation: at minimum emit spans in OTLP JSON with GenAI semconv attribute names so existing viewers work, and record the decision either way — the current position looks like drift rather than a choice, since no doc or backlog entry weighs it.

findings.title: OAuth credential rewrite drops restrictive file permissions (temp+rename with default mode)
findings.summary: The credential-refresh critical section guarded by withFileLock persists the rotated Claude OAuth access+refresh token via writeFileSync to a .tmp file with no mode option (default 0666 & ~umask, typically 0644 on POSIX) and then renameSync over ~/.claude/.credentials.json. The rename replaces whatever restrictive mode (e.g. 0600) the original credential file carried, leaving long-lived refresh tokens readable by other local users on POSIX systems; a crash between write and rename also strands a world-readable .tmp copy. The repo's OS-agnostic invariant makes the POSIX case in scope even though the primary dev platform is Windows.

findings.title: One hand-maintained boolean per analyzer decides spawn admission, and it conflates 'is this safe to run' with 'is this output noisy' — so the network-fetched binary runs by default while the repo's own pinned, CI-gated knip is denied
findings.summary: admitSpawn is six lines (src/audit/extractors/analyzers/acquisitionEngine.ts): skip -> deny, candidate.defaultRun -> admit, non-blank consent token -> admit, else deny. So the entire admission decision reduces to a per-candidate `defaultRun` boolean hand-written in src/audit/extractors/analyzers/candidates.ts. Measured: 1 of the 11 registered candidates has it true (gitleaks); the other 10 are denied absent a token, and this run's own external_analyzer_acquisition.json records exactly that — 13 of 14 status records skipped, one tool contributing. Two problems the boolean creates. (1) It does not track spawn provenance, which is the actual risk axis. The one candidate admitted without consent is a `runner: binary` candidate that resolves by downloading a pinned third-party executable and running it: the live record shows the resolved command under C:\Users\...\Temp\audit-tools-bincache\gitleaks-8.21.2\gitleaks.exe. Meanwhile knip is denied — although this repo has knip ^6.23.0 in its own devDependencies, installed at node_modules/.bin/knip, and already runs it as a release gate (check:deadcode). Approving nothing and fetching-and-executing a binary is the default; using the audited repo's own pinned, already-trusted tool requires a token. (2) The bit encodes two unrelated judgments at once. knip's own comment gives its gating reason as 'needs repo config to avoid noise ... every flag here is an unverified lead, not a confirmed finding' — a LEAD-QUALITY judgment — while the same field is documented as the run-safety/consent control. Splitting the axes fixes both: derive admission from the spawn's provenance (already-resolved local/repo-pinned tool vs a fetch of remote code -> the fetch is what needs consent), and express noisiness as a separate lead-confidence policy. That also retires the curated list itself, which is a table WE hand-maintain as the primary source in backend code — the thing the project's own standing rule bans, and which admitSpawn's docblock already disclaims ('never a maintained allowlist'). Distinct from the consent-token-semantics issue (presence check / permanence / any-string-unlocks-everything): that concerns how the token is validated, this concerns which dimension the gate keys on at all, and fixing one leaves the other in place.

findings.title: osv-scanner severity mapping matches word labels but osv-scanner emits max_severity as a numeric CVSS score string
findings.summary: parseOsvScanner maps severity by checking maxSeverity.includes('CRITICAL'|'HIGH'|'LOW'). In osv-scanner's JSON output, groups[].max_severity is the maximum CVSS *score* rendered as a numeric string (e.g. "9.8", "7.5"), not a rating word. Numeric strings never contain those substrings, so every real vulnerability falls through to the default 'medium' — a 9.8-critical dependency vulnerability is recorded at the same severity as a 4.0 one.

findings.title: recordAttemptedPackets union is an unlocked read-modify-write; a concurrent writer loses recorded attempts
findings.summary: recordAttemptedPackets reads the sidecar, unions in-memory, and rewrites the whole file with no file lock, so two writers racing on the same runDir (cooperative multi-agent peers dispatching under the same persisted run_id — the scenario the merge-side ownership gate exists for) can interleave read-then-write and one side's attempts are lost. The module's own doc states the union is load-bearing: a lost attempt makes a dispatched-and-failed packet read as never-attempted at merge, so it is deferred instead of failed, with no retry-dispatch entry and no surfaced failure.
evidence: src/audit/cli/dispatchAttempted.ts:49-51 - read, union, write with no lock; writeJsonFile makes each write atomic but not the read-modify-write sequence, so last-writer-wins erases a concurrent writer's ids.

src/audit/cli/dispatchAttempted.ts:35-43 - the doc comment states last-write-wins 'would then erase round 1's attempts, and a packet that round 1 dispatched and that failed would read as never-attempted at the next merge — deferred instead of failed', i.e. the exact loss mode the unlocked sequence still permits under concurrency.

src/audit/cli/mergeAndIngestCommand.ts:761-765 - readAttemptedPackets(runDir) is the sole authority partitionUnattemptedMissing uses to decide deferred-vs-failed, so a lost id silently converts a genuine failure into deferred work. The repo's shared withFileLock/LockedJsonStore substrate (used by the remediate state store and session-config mutator) is not applied here.

findings.title: Stale-steal TOCTOU: staleness and token are sampled non-atomically, so a freshly re-created lock can be captured as 'stale' and unlinked
findings.summary: readStaleLockToken judges staleness from stat(mtime) and then reads the token in a second, separate I/O; stealStaleLock later unlinks whenever the file content still equals that captured token, and never re-verifies the mtime after winning the claim. If a concurrent stealer completes its own steal and wx-recreates a FRESH lock between another acquirer's stat and readFile, the second acquirer captures the fresh holder's token as its 'stale token', wins the (already-released) claim, passes the content check trivially, and unlinks a live, fresh lock — a double-hold. The heartbeat cannot help: the unlink check compares content only, never mtime. The window is narrow (the stat->read gap must straddle the first stealer's unlink->recreate) but this lock guards quota-state and credential read-modify-writes, so the failure mode is concurrent writers and a lost update on those files. A cheap close: after winning the steal claim, re-stat and abort unless the mtime is still older than STALE_LOCK_MS in addition to the token match.
evidence: src/shared/quota/fileLock.ts:41-49 - staleness (stat) and identity (readFile) are two separate awaited operations; a release/steal + wx re-create landing between them makes the captured token the FRESH holder's token while the staleness verdict came from the old inode.

src/shared/quota/fileLock.ts:114-127 - the post-claim guard compares content only ('Delete it only if it STILL carries the exact stale token we observed'); when the observed token IS the fresh token, the guard passes and a live lock is unlinked. No mtime re-check exists after the claim is won.

src/shared/quota/fileLock.ts:124-125 - the claim is released in the finally immediately after the first stealer's unlink, so it is free for the second stealer at exactly the moment the race completes; interleaving: S1 claims + verifies old token; S2 stats old (stale) inode; S1 unlinks + wx-creates fresh T1; S2 reads T1; S2 claims (free), content==T1, unlinks S1's fresh lock.

findings.title: The dependency DAG declares the contract and conceptual review passes siblings of one upstream, but the linear PRIORITY scan serializes them into two round trips
findings.summary: spec/audit/dependency-map.md row for design_assessment.json lists BOTH design_review_contract and design_review_conceptual as consumers of the same single upstream, and there is no edge between the two passes. nextStepHelpers.ts handles them as two independent 'only this pass still needed' branches, and no conceptual prompt reads contract output - verified: design-review-conceptual-p1-prompt.md contains no reference to contract findings, and the two design-review-snapshots carry each pass's OWN prior_findings, never the sibling's. Yet PRIORITY hard-orders design_review_contract_completed before design_review_conceptual_completed, so the whole contract pass must complete and be ingested before the conceptual 5-way fan-out is even dispatched. Since both are host_delegation dispatch pauses over the same frozen bundle, the review phase costs two serial host round trips where one step could dispatch all six agents (1 contract + 5 perspectives) concurrently and ingest them together - roughly halving the review phase's wall time, which is the dominant phase of a deep run. The general improvement is bigger than this one pair: PRIORITY is a flat total order over an obligation set whose real constraints are a partial order, so every set of DAG-siblings is needlessly serialized. Letting the scan select a concurrently-dispatchable FRONTIER (all unsatisfied obligations with no unsatisfied ancestor) rather than a single highest-priority element preserves the 'upstream-valid before downstream-refresh' invariant exactly while recovering the parallelism the DAG already permits.

findings.title: The emitted resume command inlines a ~400-char escaped-JSON blob the host must reproduce byte-exactly
findings.summary: Every step prompt ends with the command the host must run next, and that command carries the auditor descriptor as an inline escaped-JSON literal — around 400 characters of backslash-escaped JSON, present in 6 of the recorded step prompts under .audit-tools/audit/steps/. The tool already holds this value and re-serializes it into the prompt, so the escaping is the tool's choice, not something forced by the host. This lands on the shell where it is most fragile. The repo's own conventions carry a rule for exactly this hazard (PowerShell JSON generation must be statement-safe: assign first, then pipe) and a hook guarding inline-JSON traps, on a Windows-primary machine. A grep for an alternative transport (--auditor-file, descriptor-file, auditorPath) finds none — the escaped literal is the only way in, and src/audit/cli/args.ts:246 reads it straight from the flag. This is also the auditor-agnostic invariant applied to the tool's own output: that invariant says a workflow must never depend on the host getting something right by care, and asking a host to relay 400 characters of nested escaping through an arbitrary shell is precisely such a place. It is unreadable at a glance, so a corruption in the middle of the blob is invisible until it fails to parse. Recommendation: write the descriptor to the step directory where current-step.json already lives and emit --auditor-file <path> in the prompt, keeping --auditor for programmatic callers. The emitted command becomes short enough to read and verify at a glance, and nothing has to survive a shell's quoting rules.

findings.title: A load-time guard is satisfied by keeping a knowingly-unreachable executor alive, and the unification seed cites a spec that does not exist
findings.summary: Two small items worth fixing together because both are the failure mode the gate apparatus exists to prevent, appearing inside the apparatus itself. First, FRICTION_CAPTURE_OBLIGATION_ID is a member of PRIORITY (src/audit/orchestrator/nextStep.ts:59) but is never derived by deriveAuditState, so the scan can never select it — its obligation was replaced by the terminal triage gate described in DR-017. src/audit/orchestrator/executorRunners.ts:215-218 documents this outright, saying the executor is retained for schema compatibility but is unreachable. The reason it must be retained is assertExecutorRegistryCoversPriority (nextStep.ts:71-88), a good load-time invariant requiring every PRIORITY id to own exactly one executor — which here forces dead code to stay alive to satisfy a guard about live code. The honest resolution is to remove the id from PRIORITY and delete the executor with it in one commit, per the repo's own atomic-replace rule; the guard then passes on a smaller, true registry. (DR-011's unified obligation record subsumes this: a record set cannot carry an id with no derive.) Second, the doc comment in src/shared/engine/obligationEngine.ts:18 directs the reader to spec/a3-a4-engine-unification-plan.md for the engine's design, and that file does not exist anywhere in the tree. This survives despite check:doc-code-citations, because that gate scans tracked markdown for citations into code and has no inverse — code comments citing docs are unchecked. Given how much of this codebase's reasoning lives in long comments pointing at specs, extending the existing gate to also resolve repo-path citations found in src/** comments is a small addition to a script that already owns the tracked-file resolution logic, and it closes the direction that currently rots silently.
